title: Writers: Craft & Context
publisher_platform: University of Oklahoma Libraries (OJS at journals.shareok.org); sponsored by the OU Writing Center
summary: Open access interdisciplinary journal publishing work on writers' lived experiences: personal essays about writing, research on writers, interviews, poems, and reviews.
notes: Brief described this as a University of Illinois journal; the journal's own About page names University of Oklahoma Libraries as host and the OU Writing Center as sponsor. Editors Sandra L. Tarabochia, Aja Y. Martinez, Michele Eodice. ISSN 2688-9595. Vol. 1 No. 1 published 2020 (archive runs to Vol. 6 No. 1, 2025). Mostly faculty and graduate authors, not an undergraduate journal, though Vol. 4 No. 1 (2023) includes a set of short undergraduate counterstory essays. License basis: journal-wide About page says works are distributed under 'a Creative Commons Attribution Non-Commercial License (CC BY-NC)' with authors keeping copyright (no version given); individual article pages from Vol. 2 No. 2 onward display CC BY-NC-SA 4.0.

title: Refusing to Kill My Darlings
summary: A short creative nonfiction essay in which the writer explains why she rejects the familiar advice to "kill your darlings" when revising.
notes: Vol. 2 No. 2 (2021). DOI 10.15763/issn.2688-9595.2021.2.2.6-9. License from article page. Short (4 pp.); pairs well with readings on revision.

title: On Becoming a Research Geek
summary: A novelist describes the research behind writing historical fiction, including the materials and characters involved, in a humorous and practical account.
notes: Vol. 2 No. 2 (2021). DOI 10.15763/issn.2688-9595.2021.2.2.10-16 (pages from DOI). License from article page. Useful for showing research as part of creative as well as academic writing.

title: Writing While Black
summary: An autoethnographic critical personal narrative about negotiating identity as a Black, queer writer, tracing how schooling shaped the author's relationship with writing and how an ethic of love supported healing.
notes: Vol. 2 No. 2 (2021). DOI 10.15763/issn.2688-9595.2021.2.2.30-35. License from article page. Author status not stated on page.

title: For the Love of Writing: Writing as a Form of (Self-) Love
summary: An autoethnography in which a former high school teacher describes her writing process as an act of self-love and argues that school writing instruction should help students build processes that keep them loving writing.
notes: Vol. 2 No. 1 (2021). DOI 10.15763/issn.2688-9595.2021.2.1.16-24. Author was a PhD student in Composition & Rhetoric at UW-Madison (bio in PDF). No license shown on the article page or in the PDF; license basis is the journal-wide CC BY-NC statement on the About page (version not specified).

title: Teaching ChatGPT for Grant Writing: An English Department Senior Capstone
summary: Describes a spring 2023 senior capstone that taught English majors to use ChatGPT for grant writing, with the rationale, assignment design that localizes tasks to limit AI shortcuts, classroom activities, and student process examples.
notes: Vol. 4 No. 1 (2023). DOI 10.15763/issn.2688-9595.2023.4.1.115-124. License from article page. Students in the article publish under first names/pseudonyms.

title: A Counterstory: On Eating and Belonging
summary: An undergraduate counterstory about food, Asian American identity, and belonging, written for a Counterstory Seminar Project assignment.
notes: Vol. 4 No. 1 (2023). DOI 10.15763/issn.2688-9595.2023.4.1.104-108. Undergraduate author (abstract identifies it as an undergraduate student essay). Responds to Martinez and Smith, 'Critical Theory, Critical Race Representations: Counterstory as Literary Intervention' in the same issue; works as a student model for a counterstory assignment. License from article page.

title: Young Scholars in Writing: Undergraduate Research in Writing and Rhetoric
publisher_platform: youngscholarsinwriting.org (OJS, PKP Publishing Services); supported by York College of Pennsylvania Center for Academic Innovation and Naylor Endowment in Writing Studies
summary: Peer-reviewed open access journal of undergraduate research articles in writing and rhetoric, reviewed by undergraduate students and faculty board members.
notes: Archive runs Vol. 1 (2003) to Vol. 23 (2026); founded 2003 at Penn State Berks by Laurie Grobman and Candace Spigelman (per search results; About page does not state founding). License basis: About page says 'Copyright for all content by its respective authors' and 'All materials may be reproduced for research and classroom use without permission or fee.' Article pages say individual authors retain copyright. No Creative Commons license. All articles undergraduate-authored; includes a Spotlight on First-Year Writing section and Methodological Reflections.

title: But You Are a Writer: Analyzing First-Year Composition Courses to Foster Student Confidence in Writing
summary: Using surveys and interviews across three first-year writing seminars, the author identifies four kinds of writing confidence and finds that brainstorming, professor feedback, and embedded tutoring helped students most.
notes: Vol. 22 (2025). Undergraduate author, Rider University (BA English, 2023). Copyright statement on article page: individual authors retain copyright; journal permits classroom reproduction.

title: Bridging the Gap: Adapting IMRaD to Meet Student Needs
summary: Two NYU students build a reading tool from the IMRaD structure to help students rhetorically analyze published research, test it across four knowledge domains, and report where it helps and where it confuses readers.
notes: Vol. 22 (2025). Undergraduate authors, New York University. Copyright statement on article page: individual authors retain copyright.

title: Making Confident Changes: Using Metacognitive Revision as a Pedagogical Tool
summary: Through observations of peer review sessions and questionnaire responses, the author finds that a metacognitive revision questionnaire led writers to connect revision choices to purpose, identity, and audience.
notes: Vol. 21 (2024). Undergraduate author, Oakland University (BA Writing and Rhetoric, 2023). Copyright statement on article page: individual authors retain copyright.

title: Is the Pen Mightier than the Laptop? Digital Natives and Their Preferred Writing Tools
authors: Kinkead, Joyce; Truman, Avery; Ash, Dylan; Bodell, Mason; Harvey, Jane; Lloyd, Clarissa; Miller, Ellie; Myers, Lauren; Potter, Hannah; Spence, William; Tuite, Anna; Vasquez, Isabelle; Villastrigo, Nevaeh; Corbett, Landon
summary: Students in a History of Writing course surveyed college-aged writers and analyzed essays on favorite writing implements to see whether Gen Z students prefer digital or analog writing tools.
notes: Vol. 21 (2024), Spotlight on First-Year Writing section. Utah State University class project; Joyce Kinkead (faculty) wrote the preface, Avery Truman is corresponding author. Copyright statement on article page: individual authors retain copyright.

title: Types of Peer Feedback Training, The Feedback Provider, and Performance: Toward a Process/Product Perspective
summary: A mixed-methods study comparing peer-revision and writing-center-style training for written peer feedback; neither improved scores significantly, but both groups reported better self-revision and more awareness of readers.
notes: Vol. 20 (2023). Author was an undergraduate at Georgetown University (BA English and Linguistics). Copyright statement on article pages: individual authors retain copyright.

title: Transforming Taboo: Discursive and Generic Uptake in South Asian Mental Health Recovery Narratives
summary: Applies rhetorical genre studies to recovery narratives on the Mann Mukti platform, arguing the genre turns a personal need to be heard into a shared social exigence within South Asian cultural contexts.
notes: Vol. 21 (2024). Undergraduate author, Oxford College of Emory University. Copyright statement on article pages: individual authors retain copyright.

title: Xchanges
publisher_platform: Department of English, University of New Mexico (xchanges.org)
summary: Interdisciplinary journal of technical communication, writing/rhetoric, and writing across the curriculum; the fall issue each year features upper-level undergraduate research and the spring issue features graduate student research.
notes: ISSN 1558-6456. Two issues a year; accepts articles and multimodal webtexts. Founding year not stated on site; the current editor's note says the journal is 'now in its 25th year' and the archive lists issues 1-5 as 2001-2010. Undergraduate issues confirmed by editor's notes include 13.2 (Fall 2018), 14.2 (Fall 2019), 15.2 (Fall 2020), 16.2 (Fall 2021); some recent fall issues (e.g., 19.2, a graduate teaching symposium) are not undergraduate. Site appears to have been migrated in 2026 (posts dated June-July 2026, PDFs re-uploaded under /wp-content/uploads/2026/07/). License: no Creative Commons or author-rights statement found on About, Submissions, AI Policy, or article pages; only the footer '© 2026 Xchanges · ISSN: 1558-6456 · University of New Mexico'. Treat as free-to-read, not openly licensed; license_verified false because no full copyright policy was found.

title: Students' Perceptions of Written Instructor Feedback on Student Writing
summary: Based on interviews with 12 undergraduates responding to comments on a mock paper, the study finds students value reader-based feedback, open-ended questions for developing ideas, and suggestions or examples for revision, and that the best form of feedback depends on context.
notes: Xchanges 13.2 (Fall 2018), undergraduate issue. Author was an undergraduate researcher at the University of Central Florida (issue TOC gives UCF; article says he conducted the study as an undergraduate student researcher). Web version is multi-page HTML with references and appendices; PDF also available. No open license found (site footer copyright only).

title: PragerU as Genre: How Ideologies Typify Speech
summary: A genre analysis arguing that PragerU videos imitate academic genres, much as partisan outlets imitate news, to lend credibility to ideological claims and undercut trust in academia.
notes: Xchanges 14.2. The issue page labels 14.2 'Fall 2019' (undergraduate issue per editor's note); the article page labels it 'Spring 2020'. Author institution and status not shown in the fetched page text. No open license found (site footer copyright only).

title: Creativity and Collaboration: The Relationship of Fact and Fiction in Personal Writing
summary: Starting from the author's own writing history, the essay questions the idea of creativity as solitary inspiration and examines the role of collaboration and the relationship between fact and fiction in personal writing.
notes: Xchanges 14.2 (issue page: Fall 2019; article page: Spring 2020), undergraduate issue per editor's note. Author institution not shown in the fetched page text. Includes appendices A-E. No open license found (site footer copyright only).

title: Chance (re)Collections: Twine Games and Preservation on the Internet
summary: Analyzes 20 Twine interactive-fiction games at different stages of online availability to show how digital preservation shapes which creators and communities are remembered, and discusses the limits of web archiving.
notes: Xchanges 15.2 (Fall 2020), described by the editor as the annual undergraduate issue. Author affiliation on issue TOC: University of Illinois Urbana-Champaign. No open license found (site footer copyright only).

title: Understanding the Experiences of Technical Writers in New Zealand and Australia
authors: Petersen, Emily January; Winston, Jaime; Arroyo, Uintah; Tyler, Hollye; Hayes, J. Hudd; Santy, Kelci; Jolley, Nicol; Duncan, Saxxon; West, Trevor
summary: Undergraduate technical communication students and their professor interviewed 19 technical communicators in New Zealand and Australia, finding many are self-taught and identifying key skills such as ethical decision-making, adapting to workplaces, and building writing communities.
notes: Xchanges 16.2 (Fall 2021), undergraduate issue. Weber State University; Emily January Petersen is the faculty member, the other authors are undergraduate TPC students (per article introduction). Author order follows the article page. No open license found (site footer copyright only).

title: Stylus: A Journal of First-Year Writing
publisher_platform: University of Central Florida, Department of Writing and Rhetoric, First-Year Writing Program (cah.ucf.edu)
summary: Showcases peer-reviewed writing and research by UCF students in first-year composition (ENC 1101 and ENC 1102), published twice a year.
notes: Inaugural issue 1.1 Winter 2010 (founding editor Matthew Bryan per UCF news); issue list runs to 16.2 Summer 2026, plus Knights Write Showcase special issues. Editor: Megan Lambert. Instructors submit on students' behalf. Many pieces are WAW-style literacy narratives, discourse community studies, and genre analyses citing Brandt, Gee, Swales, etc. Recent articles are web pages with embedded PDFs; PDF footers carry issue labels. License: no copyright or license statement found on the journal home, issues, or submissions pages or in the article PDFs checked (the submissions page only addresses third-party copyrighted material). Free to read; license_verified false.

title: Russhlish
parent_title: Stylus: A Journal of First-Year Writing
summary: A first-year literacy narrative about relearning Russian from an Uzbek immigrant stepmother, using Brandt's literacy sponsorship and Young's code-meshing to reflect on becoming a literacy sponsor herself as she now helps her stepmother learn English.
notes: Stylus 15.1 (Winter 2025), per the PDF running footer (the PDF filename says 14_1). Produced in Heather Vazquez's Spring 2024 ENC 1101 at UCF. 4-page PDF. Undergraduate first-year author. No license statement found.

title: Do You Understand?
parent_title: Stylus: A Journal of First-Year Writing
summary: A literacy narrative about moving from the Dominican Republic to the United States, learning English, and balancing Spanish, two family accents, and a new language and culture.
notes: Stylus 15.1 (Winter 2025), per PDF footer. Produced in Vee Kennedy's Summer 2023 ENC 1101 at UCF. Undergraduate first-year author. No license statement found.

title: A Reflective Analysis of "The True Story of the Introvert Who Wanted to Become an SLP"
parent_title: Stylus: A Journal of First-Year Writing
summary: The author reflects on her own literacy story about entering speech-language pathology as an introvert, using Gee's concept of Discourses and Mirabelli's work on workplace literacy to analyze the conflict between two of her Discourses.
notes: Stylus 15.2 (Summer 2025), per PDF footer; the issue page lists it under the shorter title 'The True Story of the Introvert Who Wanted to Become an SLP'. Produced in Melissa Ringfield's Spring 2025 ENC 1101 at UCF. Useful model of a reflective analysis paired with a literacy narrative. No license statement found.

title: The Successful Rhetoric of the TikTok Paleontology Community
parent_title: Stylus: A Journal of First-Year Writing
summary: A first-year research essay that reviews scholarship on TikTok discourse communities and analyzes how the TikTok paleontology community uses curiosity and hook strategies to spread information about prehistoric animals.
notes: Stylus 16.1 (Winter 2026), per PDF footer. Produced in Emily Proulx's Spring 2025 ENC 1102 at UCF. 16-page PDF. Draws on Duffy and on Seeley et al.'s discourse community criteria. No license statement found.

title: How Code Communicates: Rhetorical Choices in C
parent_title: Stylus: A Journal of First-Year Writing
summary: A computer science student analyzes two examples of C programming code as a genre, showing how programmers make rhetorical choices in designing and organizing code for readers.
notes: Stylus 16.2 (Summer 2026), per PDF footer. Author name printed as Maria Gabriella Fernandes Fonseca. Produced in Lissa Pompos Mansfield's Fall 2025 ENC 1101 at UCF. No license statement found.

title: Queen City Writers: A Journal of Undergraduate Writing & Composing
publisher_platform: qc-writers.com (WordPress); associated with the University of Cincinnati
summary: Refereed journal of essays and multimedia work by undergraduates at any institution, with sections for research-based inquiry essays, first-year writers, multimedia, writer snapshots, and reviews.
notes: Still active and accessible: archive runs 1.1 (Fall 2012) to 13.1 (Fall 2024, posted January 2025); site says the journal was founded in 2012. Earlier hiatus noted in a reviewer call ('after a hiatus, Queen City Writers is back'). Current submission status not confirmed. Site does not name a host; University of Cincinnati association comes from search results (UC English department journals listing) and many UC contributors. License basis: site footer and individual posts state CC BY-NC 4.0; an older site-wide notice still cites CC BY-NC 3.0 Unported. Articles are HTML posts (no PDFs).

title: Barbies Live Forever: The Linear Story of a Circular Literacy
summary: Traces how the author's storytelling literacy moved from imaginative Barbie play with her sister to an escape shaped by grief and anxiety, and back to connection through volunteering as a princess at a Ronald McDonald House.
notes: QCW 13.1 (Fall 2024), Inquiry section; posted January 3, 2025. Undergraduate author, University of Cincinnati (fourth-year honors student). License stated on the post: CC BY-NC 4.0.

title: An Appetite for Words: Developing My Literacy Palate
summary: A literacy narrative tracing the author's relationship with words from early reading and spelling bees to news and scholarly writing, and how editing a student publication pushed her past formulaic essays.
notes: QCW 12.2 (Spring 2024); issue page lists it under Storming the Gate (first-year writers), post is tagged Snapshots; posted May 24, 2024. Undergraduate author, University of Cincinnati (sophomore medical sciences major). License stated on the post: CC BY-NC 4.0.

title: Becoming Known
summary: A literacy narrative about how reading Sylvia Plath and facing a painful personal narrative assignment led the author to see vulnerability in writing as a source of connection and identity, drawing on Roozen and Scott.
notes: QCW 12.1 (Fall 2023), Snapshots section; posted January 21, 2024. Undergraduate author, Miami University (sophomore); written for a college course. License stated on the post: CC BY-NC 4.0.

title: Victor Villanueva's Bootstraps: From an Academic of Color Playlist
summary: A multimedia response to Villanueva's Bootstraps that pairs passages from the book with songs whose themes and tones echo them, arguing that multimodal composing can be a more expressive alternative to the conventional essay.
notes: QCW 12.1 (Fall 2023), Multimedia section; posted January 22, 2024. Undergraduate senior, University of North Georgia; made in an Intermediate Composition course. Playlist is hosted on Spotify (external); the post carries the written framing. License stated on the post: CC BY-NC 4.0 (site footer also shows CC BY-NC 3.0); the third-party songs themselves are not covered.

title: Dissecting Desires: A Rhetorical Analysis on Objectification in Advertising
summary: Analyzes Marc Jacobs and Ipanema ads that show isolated parts of women's bodies, arguing that framing and viewpoint position viewers as dominant, and connects these choices to objectification theory.
notes: QCW 13.1 (Fall 2024), Inquiry section; posted January 3, 2025. Author is a recent BA (English/Writing) graduate of Eastern Oregon University; the page does not say whether the essay was written for a course. License stated on the post: CC BY-NC 4.0.

title: JUMP+: The Journal for Undergraduate Multimedia Projects
publisher_platform: jumpplus.net (WordPress); maintained by Justin Hodgson, Indiana University
summary: Peer-reviewed electronic journal of undergraduate digital and multimedia course projects, each published with the assignment, course description, timeline, student reflection, and instructor reflection as a teaching resource.
notes: Started fall 2009 at UT Austin's Digital Writing and Research Lab (founder Justin Hodgson); first issue March 2010; JUMP 2.0 launched November 2012 (Issue 4.1); rebuilt as JUMP+ on WordPress after the move to Indiana University, with some early content lost. Latest issue 14.1 (December 2, 2024). As of Oct. 1, 2024 the journal is not accepting new submissions while it seeks a new editorial team; archive remains accessible. License: only the footer 'TheJUMP (c) 2016'; no license or author-rights statement on About, What is TheJUMP+, or Submissions pages. Media are often embedded from third-party hosts.

title: Treatment Talk: Expanding the Conversation Surrounding Healthcare for the Unhoused Community
parent_title: JUMP+: The Journal for Undergraduate Multimedia Projects
summary: A single-episode podcast with transcript examining limited healthcare access for unhoused people in Reno, with interviews featuring a person with lived experience and representatives of street-medicine and immunization organizations.
notes: JUMP+ Issue 14.1 (December 2, 2024). University of Nevada, Reno; Advanced Nonfiction class; instructor reflection by Bill Macauley. Includes student reflection, assignment description, course description, and timeline. No license statement found.

title: 4 Reasons RoboCop Should Be Considered a Feminist Icon
parent_title: JUMP+: The Journal for Undergraduate Multimedia Projects
summary: A video essay that applies feminist criticism to the 1987 film RoboCop and reflects on how symbols complicate the film's common reading.
notes: JUMP+ Issue 14.1 (December 2, 2024). Iowa State University; instructor reflection by Abby M. Dubisar. Made in iMovie; includes transcript and description of visuals, student and instructor reflections, assignment sheet, course description, and timeline. No license statement found.

title: Advice for First Years Exploring Education
parent_title: JUMP+: The Journal for Undergraduate Multimedia Projects
summary: A newsletter-style multimedia piece made in Canva that explains how writing is used in K-12 classrooms and what writing future teachers will be expected to produce, aimed at first-year education students.
notes: JUMP+ Issue 13.1 (January 29, 2024). University of Nevada, Reno; the issue says its projects came from Bill Macauley's 2022 Advanced Non-Fiction Writing and Writing in the Disciplines and Professions classes. Includes student reflection, assignment, and course description. No license statement found.

title: Omega Mart Ad Analysis
parent_title: JUMP+: The Journal for Undergraduate Multimedia Projects
summary: A video analysis of commercials for Meow Wolf's Omega Mart exhibit that draws on Kress and van Leeuwen and Fagerjord to show how the ads use ethos, pathos, and nostalgia.
notes: JUMP+ Issue 12.1 (October 28, 2022). Anderson University; instructor reflection by Andrew Stowe. Made in DaVinci Resolve; includes transcript and description of visuals, student and instructor reflections, assignment, course description, and timeline. No license statement found.

title: Environmental Justice in Animal Crossing New Horizons
parent_title: JUMP+: The Journal for Undergraduate Multimedia Projects
summary: A video walkthrough of the author's Animal Crossing: New Horizons island arguing that the game's ranking system rewards actions that raise eco-justice concerns, pushing players toward deforestation, colonialism, and eco-terrorism.
notes: JUMP+ Issue 12.1 (October 28, 2022). Iowa State University; instructor reflection by Abby M. Dubisar. Made with Shotcut; includes transcript and description of visuals, student and instructor reflections, assignment, and course description. No license statement found.

title: Double Helix: A Journal of Critical Thinking and Writing
publisher_platform: WAC Clearinghouse; sponsored by the College of Arts and Sciences, Quinnipiac University
summary: International, double-blind peer-reviewed pedagogy journal on links between critical thinking and writing in and across the disciplines, published annually.
notes: ISSN 2372-7497. Volume 1 (2013) through Volume 12 (2024) on the archive. Grew out of Quinnipiac's biennial critical thinking and writing conference; title comes from Ann E. Berthoff. Sections: Research Articles, Reports from the Field, The Lower Frequencies, The Provocateur, Notes, Book Reviews. License basis: journal-wide CC BY-NC-ND 4.0 statement on the Focus and Scope (policies) page and journal home page. Article PDFs on wacclearinghouse.org returned HTTP 403 to automated fetching, so article records rely on the volume pages and Crossref DOI metadata; article summaries are drawn from titles and sections, not full text.

title: ChatGPT and the Future of Writing about Writing
parent_title: Double Helix: A Journal of Critical Thinking and Writing
summary: A short Notes piece on what ChatGPT and generative AI mean for Writing about Writing courses.
notes: Vol. 11 (2023), Critical Thinking, Writing, and Artificial Intelligence; Notes section. DOI 10.37514/DBH-J.2023.11.1.09. Author affiliation (Crossref): University of Massachusetts Amherst. Pages from Crossref. PDF URL as listed on the volume page; PDF returned HTTP 403 to automated fetch, so summary is based on title and section only. License basis: journal-wide CC BY-NC-ND 4.0 statement.

title: Meaningful Writing in the Age of Generative Artificial Intelligence
parent_title: Double Helix: A Journal of Critical Thinking and Writing
summary: A Report from the Field on keeping writing assignments meaningful to students now that generative AI is widely available.
notes: Vol. 11 (2023); Reports from the Field. DOI 10.37514/DBH-J.2023.11.1.04. Authors' affiliation (Crossref): Babson College. Pages from Crossref. PDF returned HTTP 403 to automated fetch; summary based on title and section only. License basis: journal-wide CC BY-NC-ND 4.0 statement.

title: What Will Be Lost? Critical Reflections on ChatGPT, Artificial Intelligence, and the Value of Writing Instruction
parent_title: Double Helix: A Journal of Critical Thinking and Writing
summary: A brief Notes essay reflecting critically on what writing instruction might lose with the arrival of ChatGPT and artificial intelligence.
notes: Vol. 11 (2023); Notes section. DOI 10.37514/DBH-J.2023.11.1.07. Author affiliation (Crossref): Baylor University. Pages from Crossref (4 pp.). PDF returned HTTP 403 to automated fetch; summary based on title and section only. License basis: journal-wide CC BY-NC-ND 4.0 statement.

title: Teaching, Not Gatekeeping, in College Writing
parent_title: Double Helix: A Journal of Critical Thinking and Writing
summary: A two-page piece in The Lower Frequencies section arguing for teaching rather than gatekeeping in college writing courses.
notes: Vol. 12 (2024), Critical Thinking and Writing: A New Episteme; The Lower Frequencies section. DOI 10.37514/DBH-J.2024.12.1.07. Author affiliation (Crossref): Eastern Connecticut State University. Pages from Crossref. Abstract PDF: https://wacclearinghouse.org/docs/double-helix/v12/garcia-abstract.pdf. PDFs returned HTTP 403 to automated fetch; summary based on title and section only. License basis: journal-wide CC BY-NC-ND 4.0 statement.

title: Arts-Based Pedagogy to Enhance Critical Thinking in Research-Based Assignments
parent_title: Double Helix: A Journal of Critical Thinking and Writing
summary: A Report from the Field on using arts-based teaching methods to strengthen critical thinking in research-based writing assignments.
notes: Vol. 12 (2024); Reports from the Field. DOI 10.37514/DBH-J.2024.12.1.05. Author affiliation (Crossref): Appalachian State University. Pages from Crossref. Abstract PDF: https://wacclearinghouse.org/docs/double-helix/v12/hash-abstract.pdf. PDFs returned HTTP 403 to automated fetch; summary based on title and section only. License basis: journal-wide CC BY-NC-ND 4.0 statement.

title: From Novice to Apprentice: A Pedagogy for "Academic Discourse"
parent_title: Double Helix: A Journal of Critical Thinking and Writing
summary: A research article proposing a pedagogy that moves students from novice to apprentice in academic discourse.
notes: Vol. 12 (2024); Research Articles. DOI 10.37514/DBH-J.2024.12.1.02. Author affiliation (Crossref): Quinnipiac University. Pages from Crossref. Abstract PDF: https://wacclearinghouse.org/docs/double-helix/v12/katz-abstract.pdf. PDFs returned HTTP 403 to automated fetch; summary based on title and section only. License basis: journal-wide CC BY-NC-ND 4.0 statement.

title: Composition Forum
publisher_platform: Association of Teachers of Advanced Composition (with support from Penn State University)
summary: Open access journal of composition theory, pedagogy, and program profiles. Articles are HTML pages; older volumes (14.2-54) and newer volumes (55-) sit in separate archives after a 2025 move to WordPress.
notes: ISSN 1522-7502. Journal-wide license statement on the journal's Editorial Policy page: open access, contributors retain copyright, readers may use works under the Creative Commons Attribution-Share-Alike license (linked to CC BY-SA 3.0 US). Older article pages also carry a per-article footer 'Licensed under a Creative Commons Attribution-Share Alike License.' Founding year not stated on site.

title: Notes toward A Theory of Prior Knowledge and Its Role in College Composers' Transfer of Knowledge and Practice
authors: Robertson, Liane; Taczak, Kara; Yancey, Kathleen Blake
publisher_platform: Composition Forum (Association of Teachers of Advanced Composition)
summary: Proposes a theory of how college writers use prior knowledge on new writing tasks, naming three patterns: assemblage, remix, and critical incidents. Argues that how students apply what they already know can block or support transfer.
notes: Composition Forum 26, Fall 2012 (special issue on Writing and Transfer, guest ed. Elizabeth Wardle). HTML only. Page footer: 'Licensed under a Creative Commons Attribution-Share Alike License'; journal policy links CC BY-SA 3.0 US.

title: Beyond Knowledge and Skills: Writing Transfer and the Role of Student Dispositions
publisher_platform: Composition Forum (Association of Teachers of Advanced Composition)
summary: Argues that transfer research should attend to individual dispositions as well as curricula and contexts. Identifies four dispositions (value, self-efficacy, attribution, self-regulation) that can help or hinder writing transfer.
notes: Composition Forum 26, Fall 2012. HTML only. Footer: '(c) Copyright 2012 Dana Lynn Driscoll and Jennifer Wells. Licensed under a Creative Commons Attribution-Share Alike License.' Issue TOC lists second author as Jennifer Holcomb Marie Wells; article byline uses Jennifer Wells.

title: The Value of Troublesome Knowledge: Transfer and Threshold Concepts in Writing and History
authors: Adler-Kassner, Linda; Majewski, John; Koshnick, Damian
publisher_platform: Composition Forum (Association of Teachers of Advanced Composition)
summary: Uses threshold concepts to study linked general education courses in writing and history, finding shared core ideas such as audience, purpose, and genre. Shows that instructors enact these shared concepts unevenly, and suggests threshold concepts as a lens on transfer.
notes: Composition Forum 26, Fall 2012. HTML only. Footer: '(c) Copyright 2012 Linda Adler-Kassner, John Majewski, and Damian Koshnick. Licensed under a Creative Commons Attribution-Share Alike License.'

title: Selecting Genres for Transfer: The Role of Uptake in Students' Antecedent Genre Knowledge
publisher_platform: Composition Forum (Association of Teachers of Advanced Composition)
summary: Brings rhetorical genre studies, especially Anne Freadman's concept of uptake, into transfer research. Through an interview with a first-year student, shows how writers select and reshape prior genre knowledge when facing unfamiliar tasks.
notes: Composition Forum 26, Fall 2012. HTML only. Footer: '(c) Copyright 2012 Angela Rounsaville. Licensed under a Creative Commons Attribution-Share Alike License.'

title: Reflecting Back and Looking Forward: Revisiting Teaching about Writing, Righting Misconceptions Five Years On
publisher_platform: Composition Forum (Association of Teachers of Advanced Composition)
summary: Retrospective on the authors' 2007 CCC article proposing a writing-about-writing approach to first-year composition. Restates the case for teaching research-based knowledge about writing, calls on the field to name its threshold concepts, and reviews how the approach has been taken up.
notes: Composition Forum 27, Spring 2013 (Retrospective section). HTML only. Footer: '(c) Copyright 2013 Elizabeth Wardle and Doug Downs. Licensed under a Creative Commons Attribution-Share Alike License.'

title: The Difficulties of Thinking Through Freewriting
publisher_platform: Composition Forum (Association of Teachers of Advanced Composition)
summary: Challenges the assumption that freewriting is an effortless route to critical thinking. A teacher-research case study of one first-year student shows how much conversation and guidance freewriting takes, and offers classroom strategies.
notes: Composition Forum 27, Spring 2013. HTML only. Footer: '(c) Copyright 2013 Hannah Rule. Licensed under a Creative Commons Attribution-Share Alike License.'

title: Style and Substance: Templates for Academic Writing as Frames for Invention
publisher_platform: Composition Forum (Association of Teachers of Advanced Composition)
summary: Argues that templates for academic writing, such as those in They Say/I Say, need not trade substance for form. Proposes antithesis as a figure that gives students starting language while helping them invent arguments, counterarguments, and concessions.
notes: Composition Forum 55, Spring 2025. No per-article license line on the new WordPress page; journal-wide CC BY-SA 3.0 US statement on the Editorial Policy page applies.

title: Across the Disciplines
summary: Refereed open access journal on language, learning, and academic writing across the curriculum (WAC/WID/CAC), with regular and special issues. Articles are published as PDFs.
notes: Journal-wide license statement on the ATD Submissions page: articles published under a Creative Commons BY-NC-ND license (Attribution-NonCommercial-NoDerivs); authors retain copyright; no version number or license link given. Archive volumes start at Volume 1 (2004); predecessor journals Academic.Writing (2000-2003) and Language and Learning Across the Disciplines (1994-2003). The WAC Clearinghouse now lives at wacclearinghouse.org; the old wac.colostate.edu domain failed TLS handshakes during this session. Article PDFs sit behind a Cloudflare bot check, so PDF contents were not opened.

title: Student Perceptions and Use of GenAI for Writing: "Great Tool" or "Pandora's Box"?
authors: Duffy, Cheryl H.; Helens-Hart, Rose; Weigel, Stephanie M.
summary: Reports a spring 2024 survey of 226 students at a midwestern university on how they use generative AI for writing and what benefits and risks they see. Students used it often for brainstorming and revising but reported little faculty guidance and asked for clear instruction rather than bans.
notes: Across the Disciplines 22.3/4, published January 6, 2026. DOI 10.37514/ATD-J.2026.22.3-4.05. License basis: journal-wide CC BY-NC-ND statement on ATD Submissions page. PDF link taken from the volume page (PDF itself behind a bot check).

title: Faculty Expectations for Expert vs. Upper-Level Undergraduate Academic Writing
summary: Draws on 47 faculty interviews across 19 departments to compare what faculty expect of expert academic writing and of upper-level undergraduate writing. Frames undergraduate writing in the major as a phase of disciplinary enculturation, with themes of motivation, process, and imitation.
notes: Across the Disciplines 22.3/4, published January 6, 2026. DOI 10.37514/ATD-J.2026.22.3-4.02. License basis: journal-wide CC BY-NC-ND statement on ATD Submissions page.

title: Mindful Reading Beyond First-Year Writing
summary: Reports a small longitudinal, cross-institutional study of whether undergraduates carry reading practices learned in first-year writing into later courses. Aimed at writing program, WAC/WID, and writing center administrators planning cross-campus support.
notes: Across the Disciplines 22.3/4, published January 6, 2026. DOI 10.37514/ATD-J.2026.22.3-4.04. License basis: journal-wide CC BY-NC-ND statement on ATD Submissions page.

title: Writing Circles in STEM: Why Structured Peer Review Engages Students as Writers, Thinkers, and Collaborators in Their Discipline
authors: Kramer, Tereza Joy; Williams, Claire; Zeccardi, Joe; Rose, Joshua
summary: Studies kinesiology students' reflective writing from weekly, instructor-facilitated peer review groups (writing circles) on research proposals and lab reports. Finds gains in collaborative dialogue, transfer of revision strategies, and confidence as communicators and reviewers.
notes: Across the Disciplines 22.1/2, published July 25, 2025. DOI 10.37514/ATD-J.2025.22.1-2.02. License basis: journal-wide CC BY-NC-ND statement on ATD Submissions page.

title: The Box Under the Bed: How Learner Epistemologies Shape Writing Transfer
summary: Borrows Bergmann and Zepernick's 'box under the bed' metaphor to study how students' beliefs about knowledge relate to writing transfer across their undergraduate years. Identifies three types of learner epistemologies and links them to reported transfer and genre knowledge.
notes: Across the Disciplines 15.4 (July-December 2018). DOI 10.37514/ATD-J.2018.15.4.19. License basis: journal-wide CC BY-NC-ND statement on ATD Submissions page.

title: Dispositions in Natural Science Laboratories: The Roles of Individuals and Contexts in Writing Transfer
summary: Offers case studies of two science laboratories from a longitudinal study of writing transfer in the major, based on student and faculty interviews. Shows how individual dispositions and lab contexts shape whether writing knowledge transfers.
notes: Across the Disciplines 15.4 (July-December 2018). DOI 10.37514/ATD-J.2018.15.4.20. License basis: journal-wide CC BY-NC-ND statement on ATD Submissions page.

title: The WAC Journal
publisher_platform: The WAC Clearinghouse (formerly with Clemson University and Parlor Press, 2010-2025; Plymouth State University before that)
summary: Annual peer-reviewed journal on the study, theory, and teaching of writing across disciplinary and professional contexts. Free to read as PDFs on the WAC Clearinghouse.
notes: ISSN 1544-4929. Volume 1 is 1989; went national online on the WAC Clearinghouse in 2000. No Creative Commons license found. Copyright notice on journal pages: copyrighted by Clemson University (2012-2025) and Plymouth State University (1989-2011), now by editors and authors; reproduction with acknowledgment of the source 'is hereby authorized for educational use in non-profit organizations.' Article PDFs sit behind a Cloudflare bot check.

title: In Our Own Words: Adult Learners on Writing in College
authors: Fulford, Collie; Frigo, Stefanie; Abdul-Malik, Yaseen; Kelly, Thomas; Long, Adrienne; Parrish, Stuart
summary: Two faculty members and four alumni of North Carolina Central University, an HBCU, draw on adult undergraduates' own accounts of writing and learning in college. Part of a special forum on adult learners.
notes: The WAC Journal 35 (2024), Special Forum: Adult Learners. DOI 10.37514/WAC-J.2024.35.1.10. License basis: journal copyright notice (Clemson University) with reproduction authorized for nonprofit educational use; no CC license.

title: Practicing Peer Feedback: How Task Repetition and Modeling Affect Amount and Types of Feedback over a Series of Peer Reviews
authors: Bryan, Lucy; Henry, Dayna S.; Blackstone, Sarah R.; Johnson, Anna Maria; Knight, Lacie
summary: Analyzes 3,761 comments from eighty students across four peer-review sessions to see how repeated practice and model feedback change the amount and kinds of feedback students give. Suggests that repeated rounds, especially paired with models, help students become better reviewers.
notes: The WAC Journal 35 (2024). DOI 10.37514/WAC-J.2024.35.1.04. License basis: journal copyright notice with reproduction authorized for nonprofit educational use; no CC license.

title: A Middle Way for WAC: Writing to Engage
summary: Recasts writing to learn and writing in the disciplines as two ends of a spectrum and proposes writing-to-engage activities in between. Uses a revised Bloom's taxonomy to frame assignments such as applying frameworks, critiques, comparisons, and proposals.
notes: The WAC Journal 31 (2020). DOI 10.37514/WAC-J.2020.31.1.01. License basis: journal copyright notice with reproduction authorized for nonprofit educational use; no CC license.

title: Languaging Across the Curriculum: Why WAC Needs CLA (and Vice Versa)
summary: Argues that critical language awareness (CLA) gives WAC practitioners tools for what the author calls 'Languaging Across the Curriculum.' Defines CLA through three values (access, asset, agency) and applies it to WAC curricula, program design, and advocacy.
notes: The WAC Journal 34 (2023), 'Transforming WAC at 50' issue. DOI 10.37514/WAC-J.2023.34.1.06. License basis: journal copyright notice with reproduction authorized for nonprofit educational use; no CC license.

title: Prompt: A Journal of Academic Writing Assignments
publisher_platform: The WAC Clearinghouse (host since June 2023); Open Journal Systems; archived by Caltech Library via Portico
summary: Biannual, peer-reviewed open access journal that publishes academic writing assignments (prompts) from undergraduate and graduate courses in all disciplines, each with an author essay on the assignment. Aimed at faculty, WAC/WID staff, and writing program administrators.
notes: ISSN 2476-0943. Founded 2016 by co-editors Jonathan Dueck and Susanne E. Hall. License statement on the journal's About page: authors retain copyright; reuse must attribute the original and be non-commercial, under CC BY-NC 4.0 (linked). Journal record only; assignments are cataloged by another agent.

title: The Journal of Writing Analytics
publisher_platform: The WAC Clearinghouse (housed at and supported by Western Michigan University)
summary: Peer-reviewed open access journal on the computational and empirical study of writing, including corpus analysis, automated feedback, and assessment. Most articles are technical research reports suited to instructors and graduate students.
notes: ISSN 2474-7491. Volume 1 is 2017. Journal-wide license statement in the site footer: 'This work is licensed under a Creative Commons Attribution-Noncommercial-No Derivative Works 4.0 United States License' (wording as stated; no link visible; no 4.0 US port exists, so treat as CC BY-NC-ND 4.0). Copyright held by authors and editors. Article PDFs sit behind a Cloudflare bot check, so PDF contents were not opened.

title: Tracking Citation Practices Across Disciplines: A SourceMapper Analysis of MICUSP
summary: Tests three automated classifiers for identifying the rhetorical functions of citations in upper-level student papers from MICUSP, with SciBERT agreeing best with human coding. Applied to English and Biology papers, the analysis finds English papers lean on primary sources and dense citation while Biology papers draw more on secondary sources and reporting.
notes: Journal of Writing Analytics vol. 8 (2025). DOI 10.37514/JWA-J.2025.8.1.01. License basis: journal-wide CC BY-NC-ND 4.0 statement in site footer. Summary drawn from the published abstract as surfaced in search; PDF behind bot check.

title: Developing Writers' Engagement in Academic Genres: Insights from Linguistically Informed Instruction
summary: Compares 90 undergraduate writing samples to gauge how instruction based on Systemic Functional Linguistics affects students' use of engagement resources, the language that takes a stance and makes room for other views. Concludes that explicit, linguistically informed teaching strengthens rhetorical awareness and dialogic argument.
notes: Journal of Writing Analytics vol. 8 (2025). DOI 10.37514/JWA-J.2025.8.1.03. License basis: journal-wide CC BY-NC-ND 4.0 statement in site footer. Summary drawn from the published abstract as surfaced in search; PDF behind bot check.

title: Mapping the Conversation: A Social Network Perspective on Intertextual Reading and Writing
summary: Uses social network analysis to study how students in a pre-college seminar within a college access program combine curriculum texts in their writing. Draws on research on intertextuality, writing prompts, and discourse communities.
notes: Journal of Writing Analytics vol. 7 (2024). DOI 10.37514/JWA-J.2024.7.1.01. License basis: journal-wide CC BY-NC-ND 4.0 statement in site footer. Summary drawn from search-surfaced article text; findings not reviewed.

title: Literacy in Composition Studies
publisher_platform: Literacy in Composition Studies (Open Journal Systems, licsjournal.org)
summary: Refereed open access journal at the intersection of literacy studies and composition, treating literacy as socially situated and tied to power. Publishes articles, symposium essays, interviews, and reviews, with attention to marginalized, transnational, and multilingual literacies.
notes: Vol. 1 No. 1 is 2013. Copyright Notice (Submissions page): authors retain copyright; readers may use the work under the 'Creative Commons Attribution-NonCommercial-NoDerivs 4.0 Unported license' (that link points to by-nc-sa/4.0, an inconsistency). Individual article pages state 'This work is licensed under a Creative Commons Attribution-NonCommercial-NoDerivatives 4.0 International License' linked to by-nc-nd/4.0, recorded here as the operative license. Articles have DOIs (10.21623/...). No ISSN or publisher named on the About page.

title: On the Social Consequences of Literacy
summary: Asks what the consequences of literacy are and argues that composition studies, whose unit of analysis is writing, is well placed to answer. Considers how to study those consequences without reviving the oral/literate divide or losing the insights of New Literacy Studies.
notes: Literacy in Composition Studies 1.1 (2013), published 2013-03-01. DOI 10.21623/1.1.1.6. Article page: 'Copyright (c) 2013 Kate Vieira' and CC BY-NC-ND 4.0 International statement. Short piece (7 pp.).

title: Sponsoring Literacy Studies
summary: Applies Deborah Brandt's concept of literacy sponsorship to the field of literacy studies itself and to the author's own research path. Suggests that literacy builds networks of relationships that sustain literate action, and that sponsorship is itself a literate practice.
notes: Literacy in Composition Studies 1.1 (2013), published 2013-03-01. DOI 10.21623/1.1.1.3. Article page carries CC BY-NC-ND 4.0 International statement. Short piece (5 pp.); pairs well with Brandt's 'Sponsors of Literacy.'

title: Literacy/Literacies Studies and the Still-Dominant White Center
summary: Symposium response arguing, through Catherine Prendergast's critique of Shirley Brice Heath's Ways with Words, that literacy studies framed race as cultural difference and left a white center untheorized. Warns that talk of multiple literacies and discourse communities risks repeating the limits of 1990s multiculturalism.
notes: Literacy in Composition Studies 1.1 (2013), Symposium section, published 2013-03-01. DOI 10.21623/1.1.1.16. Article page carries CC BY-NC-ND 4.0 International statement. Content note: quotes a racial slur from Heath's ethnography. Summary written from the full text (3 pp.).

title: Brokering the Immigrant Bargain: Second-Generation Immigrant Youth Negotiating Transnational Orientations to Literacy
summary: Studies how children of Mexican immigrants in a New York City afterschool program understand the 'immigrant bargain,' in which parents' sacrifices are repaid through children's academic success. Argues that mentors and teachers should recognize how this narrative shapes students' autobiographical writing and goals.
notes: Literacy in Composition Studies 3.3 (2015), special issue on transnational literacies; published 2015-10-31. DOI 10.21623/1.3.3.3. Article page: 'Copyright (c) 2015 Steven Alvarez' and CC BY-NC-ND 4.0 International statement.

title: Tensions of Local and Global: South Korean Students Navigating and Maximizing US College Life
summary: Two-year ethnography of a Korean Student Association whose members came to US universities after 'Early Study Abroad.' Finds that campuses can be unwelcoming to racially and linguistically diverse students, and that members practice 'localization,' rebuilding Korean language use and networks to ground themselves as US college students.
notes: Literacy in Composition Studies 3.3 (2015); published 2015-10-31. DOI 10.21623/1.3.3.6. Article page carries CC BY-NC-ND 4.0 International statement.

title: "Kids Don't Come with Instruction Manuals": A Mother Writing to Learn Across Her Lifespan
summary: Examines the author's mother, an everyday writer whose personal journals supported her identity and work as a parent, and who plans to pass them to her children. Argues that writing to learn is lifewide and happens well outside formal schooling.
notes: Literacy in Composition Studies 12.1 (2025); published 2025-05-29. DOI 10.21623/1.12.1.2. Article page: 'Copyright (c) 2025 Anna D'Orazio' and CC BY-NC-ND 4.0 International statement.

title: Suppression on Paper, Suffering in Real Life: How Language Ideology in Nationalistic Policies Shaped the Literacy Experiences of Thai Chinese in Thailand
summary: Draws on narratives from five Thai Chinese elders to show how Phibun-era Thai nationalism, which suppressed Chinese language and schools, shaped their literacy learning in and out of school. Links language ideology to language ecology and suggests narrative inquiry as a teaching tool.
notes: Literacy in Composition Studies 12.1 (2025); published 2025-05-29. DOI 10.21623/1.12.1.3. Article page: 'Copyright (c) 2025 Nattaporn Luangpipat' and CC BY-NC-ND 4.0 International statement.

title: Journal of Teaching Writing
publisher_platform: Indiana Teachers of Writing; hosted by IU Indianapolis University Library (Open Journal Systems)
summary: Peer-reviewed journal for teachers of writing from preschool through university, covering theory and classroom practice. Published twice a year; back issues from 1982 are online as PDFs.
notes: Delayed open access, not openly licensed. About page: 'The contents of this journal become open access 24 months after publication.' Copyright Notice: 'Copyright to works published in Journal of Teaching Writing is retained by the author(s).' No Creative Commons license. ISSN 0735-1259 (print), eISSN 2374-2852. Vol. 1 No. 1 is Spring 1982. Latest issue online is Vol. 37 No. 1 (dated 2023, posted 2025-04-28), and its PDFs downloaded without login in this session.

title: Voicing Student Attitudes in Writing-About-Writing Courses: A Comparative Study
publisher_platform: Journal of Teaching Writing (IU Indianapolis University Library)
summary: Responds to calls for evidence on writing-about-writing pedagogy with a comparative study of student attitudes in WAW courses. Tests Downs and Wardle's claim that a WAW approach to first-year composition increases students' self-awareness and knowledge about writing.
notes: Journal of Teaching Writing 35.1 (2020), posted online 2022-04-07. 26-page PDF. License basis: journal Copyright Notice (authors retain copyright) plus delayed-open-access statement; no CC license.

title: Peer Review and the Writer: Teaching Students Agency
publisher_platform: Journal of Teaching Writing (IU Indianapolis University Library)
summary: Starts from students' skepticism that peer feedback is worth anything and presents classroom strategies that teach first-year writers to ask peers for the feedback they most need. Frames requesting feedback as a transferable skill for school and workplace writing.
notes: Journal of Teaching Writing 35.1 (2020), posted online 2022-04-07. Byline in PDF: Megan Lynn Isaac (Elon University context described in text). License basis: journal Copyright Notice (authors retain copyright); no CC license.

title: Lecturers, Colleagues, and Scientists: Connecting the Forms of Citation Systems to the Functions of Scholarly Roles
publisher_platform: Journal of Teaching Writing (IU Indianapolis University Library)
summary: Argues that citation systems are more than formatting rules: their forms match the scholarly roles writers take on, characterized as lecturers, colleagues, and scientists. Opens with a plagiarism controversy and draws on Bartholomae and Lea and Street's academic literacies.
notes: Journal of Teaching Writing 35.2 (2020), posted online 2022-04-07. Pages per issue table of contents. License basis: journal Copyright Notice (authors retain copyright); no CC license.

title: "Am I Up for This?": Re-Seeing a Nontraditional Student's Critical Encounters in FYC
publisher_platform: Journal of Teaching Writing (IU Indianapolis University Library)
summary: Teacher-research case study of David, a Black student in his sixties returning to college after work in the auto industry, in an inquiry-based first-year composition course. Revisits his critical encounters to ask how instructors recognize and support nontraditional students' transfer of writing knowledge.
notes: Journal of Teaching Writing 37.1 (issue dated 2023; posted online 2025-04-28, inside the stated 24-month delay, but the PDF downloaded without login). Author affiliation: Wayne State University. License basis: journal Copyright Notice (authors retain copyright); no CC license.

title: Kairos: A Journal of Rhetoric, Technology, and Pedagogy
license: Varies by webtext: author-chosen Creative Commons license where declared; otherwise author retains copyright (free access)
summary: Refereed, diamond open-access journal (first issue January 1996) that publishes born-digital scholarly webtexts on rhetoric, technology, and pedagogy, plus shorter PraxisWiki, Disputatio, and Inventio pieces.
notes: ISSN 1521-2300. About page: Kairos 'has generated a CC-BY 4.0 license for its interface design'; authors are encouraged to place a CC license on their work, and if no CC license is declared 'the author(s) retain traditional copyright to their work.' Issue index pages carry a footer saying the journal is licensed CC BY 4.0, but per the About page this covers the interface, not the webtexts. Check each webtext for its own license. No fees for authors or readers.

title: Rhetorical Roots and Media Future: How Podcasting Fits into the Computers and Writing Classroom
parent_title: Kairos: A Journal of Rhetoric, Technology, and Pedagogy
summary: A hypertext webtext paired with a seven-episode podcast series that walks through definitions of podcasting and maps the rhetorical canons, audience, purpose, and tone onto podcast composing in a writing class.
notes: Kairos 16.2 (Spring 2012), Topoi section. License statement seen on the webtext page. Episode transcripts posted as PDFs (e.g., /16.2/topoi/bowie/transcripts/rr3.pdf). The issue table of contents credits Jennifer Bowie; the webtext page itself credits her for the header/footer design.

title: Podcasting in a Writing Class? Considering the Possibilities
parent_title: Kairos: A Journal of Rhetoric, Technology, and Pedagogy
summary: Companion Praxis piece to Bowie's Topoi webtext, offering podcast types, sample podcast assignments, teaching tips, resources, and a discussion of digital-divide concerns, delivered as a webtext plus a six-episode podcast.
notes: Kairos 16.2 (Spring 2012), Praxis section. License statement seen on page; page also notes a Flickr image under CC BY-NC-SA 2.0 Generic and a public-domain illustration.

title: Where Access Meets Multimodality: The Case of ASL Music Videos
parent_title: Kairos: A Journal of Rhetoric, Technology, and Pedagogy
summary: Butler, a Deaf writer, reads ASL music videos as multimodal compositions that make sound-based meaning visually accessible, and argues that synchronizing visual, gestural, and aural modes strengthens a message and widens access. She invites students and instructors to analyze and design more inclusive compositions.
notes: Kairos 21.1 (Fall 2016), Topoi section. No CC statement found on the webtext page (checked page text and HTML), so Kairos's default author-copyright policy applies.

title: Multimodality in Motion: Disability & Kairotic Spaces
authors: Yergeau, M. Remi; Brewer, Elizabeth; Kerschbaum, Stephanie; Oswal, Sushil K.; Price, Margaret; Selfe, Cynthia L.; Salvo, Michael J.; Howes, Franny
parent_title: Kairos: A Journal of Rhetoric, Technology, and Pedagogy
summary: Eight authors argue that multimodality as commonly used implies an ableist understanding of the composer, and examine access in the informal 'kairotic spaces' of academic life, the accommodation model, and building access in from the start.
notes: Kairos 18.1 (Fall 2013), CoverWeb for the 'Accessibility and Multimodal Composition' issue. No CC statement found on the webtext index page, so default author copyright applies.

title: Suggested Practices for Syllabus Accessibility Statements
parent_title: Kairos: A Journal of Rhetoric, Technology, and Pedagogy
summary: Short, practical recommendations for writing syllabus accessibility statements that go beyond legal compliance: personalize them, place them prominently, frame access collaboratively and through Universal Design, and offer alternative assessment and delivery options.
notes: Listed in the Kairos 18.1 (Fall 2013) CoverWeb; hosted on PraxisWiki (wiki page last modified 2022). No CC statement on the page, so default author copyright applies.

title: Navigating the Soundscape, Composing with Audio
authors: Rodrigue, Tanya K.; Artz, Kate; Bennett, Julia; Carver, M.P.; Grandmont, Megan; Harris, Dan; Hashem, Danah; Mooney, Anne; Rand, Mike; Zimmerman, Amy
parent_title: Kairos: A Journal of Rhetoric, Technology, and Pedagogy
summary: Nine sonic compositions in seven genres (audio drama, oral history, audio essay, and others) from a graduate digital writing course, with the composers' reflections on voice, silence, and music, a professor's reflection, and a guide for instructors using the webtext in class.
notes: Kairos 21.1 (Fall 2016), Praxis section. No CC statement found on the webtext page, so default author copyright applies. Useful model texts for audio assignments.

title: Three Ways In: Teaching Visual Rhetoric through Web-Based Infographic Programs
authors: Lamb, Marisa Sandoval; Sheffield, Jenna; Winet, Kristin
parent_title: Kairos: A Journal of Rhetoric, Technology, and Pedagogy
summary: Three scaffolded assignments of increasing scope that use Piktochart to teach visual rhetoric through Charles Hill's framework, with an argument that constraining image and template choices prompts more critical design thinking and notes on accessibility.
notes: PraxisWiki piece listed in Kairos 21.1 (Fall 2016); wiki page says released 15 April 2016. No CC statement on page, so default author copyright applies.

title: Developing Critical Literacy and Critical Thinking through Facebook
parent_title: Kairos: A Journal of Rhetoric, Technology, and Pedagogy
summary: Describes a first-year composition unit in which students examine Facebook's interface and the human intentions behind it, arguing that social networking sites can be more natural writing spaces than course management systems.
notes: PraxisWiki piece listed in Kairos 18.1 (Fall 2013). No CC statement on page, so default author copyright applies. Some platform details are dated.

title: Computers and Composition Online
summary: Free online companion to the print journal Computers and Composition, publishing peer-reviewed webtexts in sections such as Theory into Practice, Virtual Classroom, and Professional Development.
notes: Journal-wide license: the Submissions page states 'CCO uses a Creative Commons Attribution-NonCommercial-ShareAlike License in support of the open source publishing,' and the homepage footer links to CC BY-NC-SA 3.0 (unported). Individual webtexts generally carry no separate license statement. Founding year not confirmed (archives include pieces dated 2000-2001 from its UT Austin era). The site's HTTPS certificate was expired when checked; http:// URLs work. The Elsevier print journal Computers and Composition is subscription-based and not covered here.

title: Making Waves: Voiceless Audio Essays & the Visual Rhetoric of Aural Rhetoric
summary: Using 13 audio pieces built around two student examples, Folk argues for 'voiceless' audio essays in composition classes and offers guidance for assigning and assessing them, including how applying visual rhetoric to soundwaves helps students and instructors.
notes: Listed on the CCO homepage under 'Virtual Classroom: 2015-16'; exact year not confirmed. The webtext's own page title reads 'The Visual Rhetoric of Sonic Rhetoric and the Value of the Voiceless.' A complete transcript of the audio pieces is linked from the overview (CC_visual_sonic_rhetoric_transcript.pdf). License basis: journal-wide CC BY-NC-SA statement.

title: Three Frameworks and a Pedagogical Approach: Teaching Video Arguments in First-Year Composition
summary: Lays out three frameworks and a pedagogical approach for teaching students to compose video arguments in first-year composition, with student examples.
notes: Spring 2014, Theory into Practice section. Webtext sections: introduction, three frameworks, pedagogical approach, student examples, conclusion, references. License basis: journal-wide CC BY-NC-SA statement.

title: "A Glass Case": Reading and Reflecting with GIFs
summary: Presents an assignment in which students use animated GIFs to read and reflect on texts, with sections on theory, context, assignment design, resources, student work, and outcomes.
notes: Spring 2014, Virtual Classroom section. License basis: journal-wide CC BY-NC-SA statement.

title: Image Manipulation and Ethics in a Digital-Visual World
summary: Examines the ethics of digital image manipulation through annotated examples such as retouched magazine covers and ads, altered news photographs, and viral photo hoaxes, and considers what these cases mean for teaching visual composition.
notes: Fall 2011 Special Issue: Ethics in a Digital Age. Image-rich single-page webtext. License basis: journal-wide CC BY-NC-SA statement; embedded third-party images are not covered by that license.

title: Culture Jams: Critical Media Literacy in the Digital/Multimedia Classroom
summary: Makes the case for culture jamming as a critical media literacy assignment in the digital/multimedia classroom, covering theory, the practice of jamming, and its challenges.
notes: Fall 2011 Special Issue: Ethics in a Digital Age. Webtext sections: intro, theory, jamming, challenges, conclusion, references. License basis: journal-wide CC BY-NC-SA statement.

title: Teaching Accessible Design Through Critical Making and Board Games
summary: Describes a board-game re-design project that uses critical making and attention to materiality to teach accessible design, drawing on accessibility scholarship in game design.
notes: Fall 2022 Special Issue: Making Games Matter: Games and Materiality. License basis: journal-wide CC BY-NC-SA statement.

title: Considerations for Creative Commons Licensing of Open Educational Resources: The Value of Copyleft
summary: Weighs the CC Attribution and Attribution-ShareAlike licenses for open educational resources and, drawing on open-source practice and rhetorical theory, argues that ShareAlike (copyleft) better sustains an education commons.
notes: Dated September 2010 on the webtext; listed under Fall 2010-Spring 2011, Theory into Practice. License basis: journal-wide CC BY-NC-SA statement. Directly relevant to an OER textbook builder.

title: Present Tense: A Journal of Rhetoric in Society
publisher_platform: presenttensejournal.org (WordPress; HTML pages with article PDFs)
summary: Peer-reviewed, open-access online journal of rhetoric in society that publishes short articles on contemporary social, cultural, political, and technological issues, with themed issues on platforms, medical rhetoric, and race.
notes: License basis (Submissions page, 'Copyright Information - Creative Commons'): 'Present Tense is an open access journal... We use the Creative Commons Attribution-Noncommercial-Share Alike 3.0 United States License for our journal'; authors retain copyright. This is BY-NC-SA, not BY-NC-ND as initially assumed. Individual article pages and PDFs show no per-article license; site footer reads 'Copyright (c) 2026.' Inaugural issue Vol. 1, Issue 1 (editorial dated September 8, 2010).

title: Building Dark Patterns into Platforms: How GamerGate Perturbed Twitter's User Experience
parent_title: Present Tense: A Journal of Rhetoric in Society
summary: Analyzes how GamerGate linked Twitter with other platforms into a coordinated network that used dark patterns to trap targets and mislead participants, drawing on a sample of 100 tweets from November 2014.
notes: Vol. 6, Issue 3 (2018), Special Issue on the Rhetoric of Platforms; posted January 21, 2018. PDF header reads 'Present Tense, Vol. 6, Issue 3, 2018.' License basis: journal-wide CC BY-NC-SA 3.0 US statement.

title: Corporate Kairos and the Impossibility of the Anonymous, Ephemeral Messaging Dream
parent_title: Present Tense: A Journal of Rhetoric in Society
summary: Argues that anonymous, disappearing-message apps struggle to survive in advertising-driven social media, comparing Snapchat, which paired ephemeral messaging with advertiser-friendly public content, with Yik Yak, which declined after adding user identities and shut down in 2017.
notes: Vol. 6, Issue 3 (2018), Special Issue on the Rhetoric of Platforms; posted January 20, 2018. PDF link taken from the article page. License basis: journal-wide CC BY-NC-SA 3.0 US statement.

title: Constructing Research, Constructing the Platform: Algorithms and the Rhetoricity of Social Media Research
parent_title: Present Tense: A Journal of Rhetoric in Society
summary: Argues that social media researchers must account for nonhuman actors, especially algorithms, that shape both platforms and research results, using Twitter bots and Facebook's personalized search as examples and closing with reflexive questions for researchers.
notes: Vol. 6, Issue 3 (2018), Special Issue on the Rhetoric of Platforms; posted January 23, 2018. PDF link taken from the article page. License basis: journal-wide CC BY-NC-SA 3.0 US statement.

title: Representation, Resistance, and Rhetoric: Bananas Catalyze Campus Activism
authors: Dubisar, Abby M.; Roesch-McNally, Gabrielle E.
parent_title: Present Tense: A Journal of Rhetoric in Society
summary: Uses student activism against a genetically modified banana developed at Iowa State University for Uganda as a case for teaching food-systems rhetoric, arguing that local cases help students analyze how their own universities frame agriculture and hunger.
notes: Vol. 7, Issue 1 (2018), 'Identity, Inclusion, and Social Justice'; posted May 4, 2018. PDF link taken from the article page. License basis: journal-wide CC BY-NC-SA 3.0 US statement.

title: I'll Google It!: How Collective Wisdom in Search Engines Alters the Rhetorical Canons
parent_title: Present Tense: A Journal of Rhetoric in Society
summary: Argues that web searching is collaborative because Google's rankings depend on many users' links and choices, and uses examples such as 'Google bombing' to rethink the classical rhetorical canons for shared authorship.
notes: Vol. 1, Issue 1 (2010); posted August 1, 2010. PDF link taken from the article page. Search examples are dated but the canon framework still teaches well. License basis: journal-wide CC BY-NC-SA 3.0 US statement.

title: Technical Communication and Social Justice
publisher_platform: Open Journal Systems, hosted by East Carolina University (techcommsocialjustice.org)
summary: Interdisciplinary, peer-reviewed, open-access journal (TCSJ) publishing biannually on social justice in technical communication research, teaching, and activism; first volume 2023.
notes: Copyright notice (Submissions page): 'TCSJ is a peer-reviewed, open access, online journal... Contributing authors retain copyright to their work... We ask that readers use the works published in TCSJ freely while attributing authorship.' Article pages each state 'This work is licensed under a Creative Commons Attribution-NonCommercial-NoDerivatives 4.0 International License' with author copyright. Vol. 1 No. 1 (2023) through Vol. 4 No. 1 (2026) in archive. PDF download URLs follow /article/download/{id}/{galley} (verified on one article).

title: Looking "Under the Hood" of SEO Conversion: Paradoxical Goals and Moral Dilemmas Faced by the Digital Age Rhetorician
summary: Argues that writers in technical, SEO, and social media roles must understand search engines' hidden practices, since uncritical reliance on them can reinforce harm to marginalized groups, and offers teaching approaches.
notes: Vol. 3 No. 1 (2025), Special Issue on Digital Activism, Pedagogy, and Advocacy; published 2025-05-02. License and 'Copyright (c) 2025' author notice seen on article page. PDF (22 pp.) verified.

title: Interest-Driven Public Networks and Writing Pedagogy: Reframing and Harnessing Digital Spaces as Activism Playgrounds
summary: Proposes 'interest-driven public networks' as a framework for how personal passions and strategic goals online build civic engagement, and offers a writing pedagogy that treats everyday platforms as sites for practicing activism across technical communication and first-year composition.
notes: Vol. 3 No. 1 (2025), Special Issue on Digital Activism, Pedagogy, and Advocacy; published 2025-05-02. License seen on article page. PDF URL built from the galley ID using the download pattern verified on another TCSJ article.

title: A Digital-Decolonial Approach to Writing Pedagogy
summary: Proposes a writing pedagogy combining digital rhetoric, intersectionality, and decoloniality, arguing it serves students historically underrepresented in classrooms and curricula, especially in online settings.
notes: Vol. 3 No. 1 (2025), Special Issue on Digital Activism, Pedagogy, and Advocacy; published 2025-05-02. License seen on article page. PDF URL built from the galley ID using the verified download pattern.

title: The Invisible Work of Iterative Design in Addressing Design Injustices
summary: Argues that technical communication's design-based problem solving rarely addresses oppression, and proposes iterative design built on non-linearity, slowness, and multivocal critical imagination for classrooms, institutions, and communities.
notes: Vol. 1 No. 2 (2023), Summer Issue; published 2023-05-28. License and 'Copyright (c) 2023' author notice seen on article page. PDF URL built from the galley ID using the verified download pattern.

title: Teaching Editing for Social Justice
summary: Reports on a professional editing course redesigned around social justice; content analysis of students' early and final definitions of editing shows a shift from copyediting toward author relationships, rhetorical awareness, and substantive editing.
notes: Vol. 1 No. 2 (2023), Summer Issue; published 2023-05-28. License seen on article page. PDF URL built from the galley ID using the verified download pattern.

title: Programmatic Perspectives
publisher_platform: Council for Programs in Technical and Scientific Communication (CPTSC); Open Journal Systems (programmaticperspectives.cptsc.org)
summary: Peer-reviewed, biannual CPTSC journal for administrators and faculty in technical and professional communication programs, covering curriculum, program administration, pedagogy, and faculty issues; free to read online.
notes: Article pages in the OJS archive (Vol. 13, 2022 onward) each state 'This work is licensed under a Creative Commons Attribution-NonCommercial 4.0 International License' with author copyright. The Submissions copyright notice adds: 'The CPTSC grants colleges, universities, and libraries permission to use materials published in Programmatic Perspectives free of charge for educational purposes.' Older volumes (before Vol. 13) are not in this OJS archive and were not checked. Founding year not confirmed. Mostly instructor-facing; PDF download URLs follow /article/download/{id}/{galley} (verified on one article).

title: Artificial Intelligence, Large Language Models, and Design Thinking in TPC Classrooms
authors: Masters-Wheeler, Christine; Bay, Jennifer; Sullivan, Patricia
summary: Asks how technical and professional communication programs can bring AI models into the curriculum while keeping rigor and ethics, and proposes design thinking as the framework for teaching ethical, iterative AI use.
notes: Vol. 14 No. 2 (2023), Research Articles; posted online 2024-02-05 (year field uses volume year). Special issue on design and design thinking. License and 'Copyright (c) 2024' author notice seen on article page. PDF URL built from galley ID using the verified download pattern.

title: Experience Architecture: Developing an Interdisciplinary UX Undergraduate Degree
authors: McArdle, Casey; Potts, Liza; Tegtmeyer, Rebecca
summary: Program showcase on building a shared, humanities-grounded undergraduate user experience program across two departments, including the questions behind its 2013 launch and 2020 revision as Experience Architecture.
notes: Vol. 14 No. 2 (2023), Program Showcases; posted 2024-02-05. License seen on article page. PDF URL built from galley ID using the verified download pattern.

title: Online Design Thinking and Community-Based Learning: Co-Designing an Indigenous Curriculum to Help Redress Language Marginalization
summary: Case study of an online design thinking project in which participants worked with an Indigenous organization in Hueyapan, Morelos, Mexico, to co-design a curriculum for teaching Nahua to young people, proposing a TPC pedagogy of radical collaboration.
notes: Vol. 14 No. 2 (2023), Research Articles; posted 2024-02-05. License seen on article page. PDF URL built from galley ID using the verified download pattern.

title: Audience Personas: Audience Analysis Documentation for Rhetorical Technical Communications
summary: Offers a template for documenting audience personas, drawn from technical content marketing and UX practice, as a practical way to turn audience analysis into a shared reference for writers, editors, and designers.
notes: Vol. 15 No. 1 (2024), FOCUS section; published 2024-08-05. License seen on article page. PDF verified (about 10 pp.). Short and usable as a student reading.

title: Leveraging Design Thinking and Generative AI to Transform TPC Pedagogy
summary: Commentary urging TPC instructors to use generative AI tools to teach design thinking, with examples of ChatGPT activities from undergraduate technical communication courses for engineering majors.
notes: Vol. 15 No. 1 (2024), Commentaries; published 2024-08-05. License and 'Copyright (c) 2023' author notice seen on article page. PDF URL built from galley ID using the verified download pattern.

title: Journal of Multimodal Rhetorics
summary: Fully online, open-access, peer-reviewed journal (JoMR) publishing essays, demonstrations, and multimodal projects on multimodality and rhetoric.
notes: ISSN 2472-7318. Journal-wide license statement on homepage and article footers: 'Authors retain copyright to their individual essays via Creative Commons Attribution 4.0 International Licenses.' Issues 1.1 through 10.1; founding year not stated on site. Article pages give no dates; issue 5.2 is labeled Fall 2021.

title: Writing as Designing: Integrating Infographics in Composition
summary: Studies students in an advanced composition course who made research infographics, using interviews and their products to show how design work builds metacognitive awareness of visual choices, and offers a heuristic for instructors and students.
notes: JoMR 5.2 (Fall 2021), Discussions section. License statement in page footer. PDF verified (19 pp.).

title: Musical Listening: Addressing the Rhetoric of Music in Sonic and Multimodal Composition
summary: Proposes 'Musical Listening,' a classroom heuristic that applies musical expectation theory to speech, prose, and instrumental music so students can analyze and compose with sonic rhetoric, and describes assignments for sound-only and multimodal projects.
notes: JoMR 5.2 (Fall 2021), Discussions section. License statement in page footer. PDF path taken from the article page.

title: Slow Looking: Sitting with the Black Lives Matter Murals of Downtown Raleigh
summary: Applies a slow-looking method to the temporary Black Lives Matter murals painted on plywood in downtown Raleigh in 2020, documenting them as protest art and counterdata while reflecting on the author's position as a white educator.
notes: JoMR 5.2 (Fall 2021), Demonstrations section. License statement in page footer. PDF path taken from the article page. Image-rich; good model for visual analysis.

title: artifact: a comic essay about a revision of a revision assessment rubric for student writing
summary: A comic essay on revising a rubric for assessing revision in an advanced community college ESOL writing course, finding that extended revision time, regular feedback checks, and co-designed rubrics build students' confidence in revising.
notes: JoMR 5.2 (Fall 2021), Discussions section. License statement in page footer. PDF path taken from the article page. Doubles as a model of scholarly comics.

title: enculturation: a journal of rhetoric, writing, and culture
summary: Anonymously refereed journal of rhetoric, writing, and culture founded in 1996, publishing articles, sonic projects, responses, reviews, and the Intermezzo ebook series.
notes: Copyright page: 'enculturation is published under an Attribution-NonCommercial-ShareAlike Creative Commons License' and 'Authors will retain copyrights to their material.' The site's license badge links to CC BY-NC-SA 3.0, and each article page repeats the license line. Founded at the University of Texas at Arlington by Byron Hawk and David Rieder (About page). Articles are dated individually and grouped into numbered issues.

title: Reading Mean Comments to Subvert Gendered Hate on YouTube: Toward a Spectrum of Digital Aggression Response
parent_title: enculturation: a journal of rhetoric, writing, and culture
summary: Argues that women YouTubers who read hateful comments aloud and answer with parody can weaken gendered harassment and rally their communities, and proposes a spectrum of direct-to-indirect responses shaped by a creator's race, gender, and privilege.
notes: Published March 16, 2021; listed in enculturation Issue 34. License line seen on article page.

title: The View from 'Zoom University': Surveillance and Control in Higher Ed's Pandemic Pedagogy Pivot
parent_title: enculturation: a journal of rhetoric, writing, and culture
summary: Argues that the pandemic move to Zoom intensified the surveillance and control already built into educational technology, and calls for 'counter-declarations' and collective alternatives while noting that the burdens fall unevenly by race, class, and gender.
notes: Published February 10, 2022; listed in enculturation Issue 34. License line seen on article page.
