title: Of Sound, Bodies, and Immersive Experience: Sonic Rhetoric and its Affordances in The Virtual Martin Luther King Project
authors: Gallagher, Victoria J.; Rosenfeld, Cynthia; Tomlison, Conner
parent_title: enculturation: a journal of rhetoric, writing, and culture
summary: Argues that sound works as material rhetoric that shapes listeners' sense of presence, proposing locative, generative, and comparative functions of sound and drawing on student responses to the Virtual Martin Luther King Project.
notes: Published May 16, 2022; listed in enculturation Issue 34. Byline spells 'Conner Tomlison' (body text spells 'Tomlinson'). License line seen on article page.

title: Sound Judgments: A Case Study in Digital Ethos and Networked Phronesis
parent_title: enculturation: a journal of rhetoric, writing, and culture
summary: Shows how repeated jargon on music-cataloging sites like Rate Your Music hardens into a communal standard of credibility, and proposes 'networked phronesis' as a more generative, community-minded way to build ethos online.
notes: Published February 10, 2022; listed in enculturation Issue 34. License line and CC BY-NC-SA 3.0 badge seen on article page.

title: Carried from Home on the Thread of a Tune: Listening for Misunderstanding
authors: Cushman, Jeremy; Crook, Andrew; Kelly, Shannon
parent_title: enculturation: a journal of rhetoric, writing, and culture
summary: A sonic project, with a written essay and PDF transcript, that treats listening as effortful rhetorical work, layering student voices, musical interruptions, and allusions into a deliberately slow argument.
notes: Sonic Projects section; published March 25, 2022; listed in enculturation Issue 34. Author order differs: homepage lists Cushman, Crook, Kelly; the article page lists Crook, Cushman, Kelly. Page links a transcript (carried_transcript.pdf). License line seen on article page.

title: Journal of Response to Writing
publisher_platform: Brigham Young University ScholarsArchive (Digital Commons); funded by BYU Department of Linguistics and College of Humanities
summary: Peer-reviewed, fully open-access journal on teacher, peer, tutor, and automated response to writing, with a strong second-language writing strand. Issues include featured research articles, teaching articles, and short Teaching Tips.
notes: About page: founded 2014 by Dana Ferris, Norm Evans, James Hartshorn, and Grant Eckstein; Vol. 1 Iss. 1 is 2015; two issues a year through Vol. 12 Iss. 1 (2026). ISSN 2575-9809. No Creative Commons license on the journal, policy, or article pages; the Submission Guidelines & Policies page says authors are the initial owners of the copyrights to their works. No fees to readers or authors. The domain journalrw.org does NOT belong to the journal (it is an unrelated blog about journals); use the ScholarsArchive URL. Direct PDF links (cgi/viewcontent.cgi) returned HTTP 403 to automated fetching but are the links listed on the issue pages.

title: "I Don't Understand What You're Saying!": Lessons from Three ESL Writing Tutorials
summary: Three case studies of writing center tutorials with newly arrived ESL writers, looking at tutor strategies and whether students met their goals. The quality of tutor-student dialogue mattered more than the number of corrections, and the writers needed explicit metalanguage to say what they wanted.
notes: Vol. 1, Iss. 1 (2015), Article 4 (Featured Articles). Author affiliation: Andrews University. Keywords: writing center, scaffolding, ESL writers, second language writing. License basis: journal policy page (authors own copyright); no CC license shown.

title: Commenting across the disciplines: Partnering with writing centers to train faculty to respond effectively to student writing
summary: Describes a faculty development program in which new faculty meet with experienced undergraduate writing tutors to review their comments on first-year student writing. The aim is feedback that asks questions and sets up conversation, and the piece argues for writing center partnerships beyond one-on-one tutoring.
notes: Vol. 1, Iss. 1 (2015), Article 5 (Teaching Article). Author affiliation: Pitzer College. Keywords: writing centers, tutors, faculty development, commenting, first-year writing, conferencing. Also usable in peer tutoring courses to show tutors' expertise. License basis: journal policy page.

title: Composition Students' Opinions of and Attention to Instructor Feedback
summary: Two years of survey data from composition students on whether they read instructor feedback, what prompts them to, and what they find useful. Students were grade-driven but wanted to improve, and were more motivated when they could revise and when comments were clear, individualized, and positive.
notes: Vol. 5, Iss. 1 (Winter 2019), Article 3 (Featured Articles). Author affiliation: Kent State University. Keywords: instructor feedback, comments, survey, qualitative analysis. Works as a WAW reading on how students use comments. License basis: journal policy page.

title: Preparing Students to Engage With Teacher Feedback
summary: A short Teaching Tip on getting students ready to receive and work with teacher feedback, with attention to the emotions feedback can raise.
notes: Vol. 8, Iss. 1, Article 5 (Teaching Tips). Issue is labeled 2021, but the page's recommended citation gives 2022; year recorded as the issue year. Keywords: emotions, teacher feedback. No abstract on the landing page; summary is based on title, keywords, and section. License basis: journal policy page.

title: Using "Compare Documents" to Facilitate Substantive Revision and Reflection
summary: A Teaching Tip on using a word processor's Compare Documents feature to push students toward substantive revision and reflection on what they changed.
notes: Vol. 10, Iss. 2 (2024), Article 5 (Teaching Tips). Author affiliation: University of Michigan. Keywords: feedback, substantial revision, reflection. No abstract on the landing page; summary is based on title and keywords. License basis: journal policy page.

title: Feedback Menus: Expanding Student Choice in Response to Writing
summary: Describes the Feedback Menu, a protocol that lets students choose the focus and mode of the feedback they get, meant to build agency and feedback literacy at any stage of drafting. Includes implementation steps, sample menu items, and notes for face-to-face and online courses.
notes: Vol. 12, Iss. 1 (2026), Article 6 (Teaching Tips). Author affiliation: University of California, Davis. Keywords: feedback literacy, student agency, feedback strategy. License basis: journal policy page.

title: The Writing Center Journal
publisher_platform: Purdue University Press via Purdue e-Pubs (Digital Commons); flagship journal of the International Writing Centers Association (IWCA)
summary: The IWCA's peer-reviewed flagship journal of writing center research, launched in 1980 by Lil Brannon and Stephen North. The full run, Vol. 1 (1981) through the current volume, is free to read on Purdue e-Pubs.
notes: Free access, not openly licensed. The Submission Guidelines say authors assign all copyright to Purdue e-Pubs (personal-use exceptions); reuse requires credit to Purdue e-Pubs as copyright holder. No Creative Commons statement on journal or article pages. Site header labels it a Purdue University Press Open Access Journal; all-issues page lists Vol. 1 (1981) to Vol. 44 Iss. 1 (2026). Some older issues show a volume year that differs from the article's recommended-citation year (e.g., Vol. 12 shown as 1992 but cited as 1991). ISSN 2832-9414; DOIs use prefix 10.7771/2832-9414. Also indexed in JSTOR. Direct PDF links returned HTTP 403 to automated fetching but are the download links shown on article pages.

title: Collaboration, Control, and the Idea of a Writing Center
summary: A widely taught essay on competing models of the writing center and what genuine collaboration between writers and tutors requires. A standard reading in peer tutoring courses.
notes: Vol. 12, Iss. 1, Article 3. DOI 10.7771/2832-9414.1252. Recommended citation on the page gives 1991; the issue breadcrumb says Vol. 12 (1992). No abstract on landing page; summary describes the essay's well-known subject. License basis: journal submission guidelines (copyright assigned to Purdue e-Pubs).

title: Multi-cultural Voices: Peer Tutoring and Critical Reflection in the Writing Center
authors: Okawa, Gail Y.; Fox, Thomas; Chang, Lucy J.Y.; Windsor, Shana R.; Chavez, Frank Bella, Jr.; Hayes, LaGuan
summary: A six-author piece on peer tutoring and critical reflection in a multicultural writing center.
notes: Vol. 12, Iss. 1, Article 4. DOI 10.7771/2832-9414.1253. Recommended citation gives 1991; issue breadcrumb says 1992. The landing page lists no affiliations, so whether the co-authors were peer tutors is not confirmed here (check the PDF). No abstract on landing page. License basis: journal submission guidelines.

title: Revisiting "The Idea of a Writing Center"
summary: North's follow-up to his 1984 College English essay "The Idea of a Writing Center," reconsidering his earlier claims about the writing center's role. Often paired with the original in tutor-education courses.
notes: Vol. 15, Iss. 1, Article 3. DOI 10.7771/2832-9414.1313. Recommended citation gives 1994; issue listed as Vol. 15 (1995). No abstract on landing page. License basis: journal submission guidelines.

title: A Critique of Pure Tutoring
authors: Shamoon, Linda K.; Burns, Deborah H.
summary: Questions the orthodoxy of non-directive tutoring and makes a case for more directive, modeling-based approaches in some situations. A common counterpoint reading in peer tutoring courses.
notes: Vol. 15, Iss. 2 (1995), Article 5. DOI 10.7771/2832-9414.1287. No abstract on landing page; summary describes the essay's well-known argument. License basis: journal submission guidelines.

title: Centering AI Literacy: Exploring Brazilian International Students' Perceptions of ChatGPT and Peer Tutoring
authors: Dunning, Leigh Ann; Leal, Raissa Borges De Oliveira
summary: Case study of undergraduate Brazilian international students at a small liberal arts college who got feedback from both peer tutors and ChatGPT. They valued tutors' human connection and rhetorical help and used ChatGPT for quick, nonjudgmental help with multilingual challenges.
notes: Vol. 43, Iss. 3 (2025), Article 6. DOI 10.7771/2832-9414.2110. Both authors listed with Stetson University affiliation. License basis: journal submission guidelines.

title: Neurodivergent Peer Tutoring and Anti-Ableism: Two High Schoolers' Lived Experiences While Working in a Neurodiversity-Based Writing Center
summary: Multiple case study of two neurodivergent high school students who tutored neurodivergent peers in a special education school's writing center, read through critical disability theory. Findings challenge stereotypes such as a lack of empathy and question routine practices like reading aloud.
notes: Vol. 44, Iss. 1 (2026), Article 3. DOI 10.7771/2832-9414.2135. Author affiliation: New Vistas School. License basis: journal submission guidelines.

title: Praxis: A Writing Center Journal
publisher_platform: University Writing Center, The University of Texas at Austin (praxisuwc.com); archive also in UT's Texas ScholarWorks repository
summary: Peer-reviewed online writing center journal published by UT Austin's University Writing Center, with columns, focus articles, and book reviews. Articles are published as free HTML pages, and some columns are written by peer consultants.
notes: Founded 2003; peer review adopted 2011; three issues a year (Fall, Spring, Summer). No Creative Commons license. Policies page: Praxis provides immediate open access; 'Permission for electronic dissemination of Praxis is granted'; reproduction in print for educational purposes by non-profit organizations such as libraries and schools is permitted; other uses require permission (praxisuwc@gmail.com). Recorded as 'All rights reserved (free access)' because no open license is named, but the stated permissions cover nonprofit educational print and electronic distribution. The back-issues page warns some older links are broken. The UT Texas ScholarWorks collection (repositories.lib.utexas.edu/collections/6cdc78e5-c898-4093-82a9-10b0eab56697) returned HTTP 403 to automated fetching, so its rights statements were not checked.

title: Closing the Gap: A Practical Guide to Science in the Writing Center
summary: Describes how Barnard's writing center built a science-specific program with trained undergraduate Science Fellows. Offers a practical guide to common concerns in science writing (clarity, organization, scientific tone) and tutoring strategies for science students.
notes: Vol. 17, No. 1 (2019), Columns section; about 3,000 words. Author bio (171-about-the-authors): B.A. in Neuroscience and Behavior from Barnard, three years on the Barnard Writing Center staff as a student, then first Coordinator of the Science Fellows program. Surname spelled 'Schome' in the author bio and table of contents but 'Shome' in the article byline. Former undergraduate consultant author. License basis: Praxis policies page.

title: "I Was Kind of Angry": Understanding Resistance to Feedback in Two Tutor Education Courses
authors: Bleakney, Julia; Mattison, Michael; Ryan, Jennifer
summary: Tutors-in-training at two schools exchanged and commented on each other's papers and were then interviewed about being on the receiving end. Getting feedback made them more aware of writer resistance and of the need to tailor their own comments with care.
notes: Vol. 17, No. 1 (2019), Focus Articles. The table of contents lists the title as "'I was kind of angry': Tutors Receiving Feedback in Order to Understand Writer Resistance"; the title above is from the article page. Affiliations: Elon University, Wittenberg University, University of Dayton. Author bio: Jennifer Ryan was a former undergraduate advisor (tutor) at the Wittenberg Writing Center (B.A. 2019). License basis: Praxis policies page.

title: "I Believe This is What You Were Trying to Get Across Here": The Effectiveness of Asynchronous eTutoring Comments
authors: Buck, Courtney; Spallino, Jamie; Nolan, Emily
summary: Analyzes tutor side comments and the revisions they prompted in 46 resubmitted eTutoring papers at a liberal arts writing center. About 55% of directive comments were effective, formal comments worked best, and sayback (reader-response) comments could still prompt revision.
notes: Vol. 18, No. 2 (2021), Focus Articles. All three authors at Wittenberg University; the article describes them as tutors (some in training when the study began) at a center staffed by undergraduate advisors, so they were likely undergraduate tutors, but no bio confirming this was found (the issue's about-the-authors page returned 404). License basis: Praxis policies page.

title: "How I Speak Doesn't Really Matter; What I Speak About Does": BIPOC Tutor Voices on Linguistic Justice in the Writing Center
summary: Interviews with three BIPOC undergraduate tutors at a Minority Serving and Hispanic Serving Institution about how they understand and practice linguistic justice. Identity, belonging, multilingualism, and authentic voice shape their approaches, and the authors call for contextualized implementation that recognizes tutors' emotional labor.
notes: Vol. 22, No. 3 (2025), Focus Articles. Authors are writing center administrators (Claremont McKenna College; University of California, Merced); the piece centers undergraduate tutor voices. Table of contents punctuates the title with a comma rather than a semicolon. License basis: Praxis policies page.

title: Introverts Achieving Confidence in the Writing Center: A Guide for Consultants
summary: A short guide for consultants on supporting introverted writers: balancing feedback with reassurance, sharing one's own writing struggles, and keeping a welcoming presence. Also describes how the author's center uses its quiet space and seating to put writers at ease.
notes: Vol. 23, No. 1 (2025), Column Essays; about 1,000 words. Author bio: student at Pfeiffer University (Health and Exercise Science) working as a peer tutor and writing center consultant; undergraduate tutor author. License basis: Praxis policies page.

title: What is Too Much Help from GenAI?
summary: Argues that writing centers risk sliding back into the old fix-it-shop model if generative AI does students' writing for them. Proposes the heuristic "If I, the tutor, could do X, should I?" and finds chatbots acceptable for source retrieval or as reverse dictionaries but not for handing over finished answers.
notes: Vol. 23, No. 1 (2025), Column Essays; about 1,400 words. Author: Writing Center Assistant Director, University of Arkansas - Fort Smith. Short and discussable in FYC or tutoring courses. License basis: Praxis policies page.

title: The Peer Review
publisher_platform: International Writing Centers Association (IWCA); hosted by the WAC Clearinghouse (migrating from thepeerreview-iwca.org)
summary: Open-access, multimodal IWCA journal that publishes emerging writing center researchers, including graduate, undergraduate, and high school authors. Articles are free HTML web texts.
notes: Journal-wide license statement on the journal's own WAC Clearinghouse page: copyright held by authors and editors; works licensed under Creative Commons Attribution-NonCommercial-NoDerivatives 4.0 International. ISSN 3143-9004. First issue is Issue 0 (Autumn 2015) per the issues archive; current issue 10.2 (Winter 2026). The legacy WordPress site (thepeerreview-iwca.org) still hosts back issues and shows no license on article pages; the journal says it is transitioning to the WAC Clearinghouse, so legacy URLs may move. License recorded from the journal-wide statement.

title: Tutoring Controversial Topics in the Writing Center
summary: An undergraduate tutor reflects on avoiding a session about a controversial thesis early on and argues that tutors need strategies for politically charged writing, especially online. Includes an annotated bibliography of 25 resources and proposals for future research.
notes: Issue 5.1 (Summer 2021). Author affiliation: Lewis University; the author describes himself as an undergraduate tutor. About 2,000 words. License basis: journal-wide CC BY-NC-ND 4.0 statement on wacclearinghouse.org/tpr/ (no license shown on the legacy article page).

title: Tutor Metamorphosis: Expectations and Reality when Tutoring Remotely
authors: Tondy, Emily; Gelet, Alyssa; Wetzl, Ana
summary: Two English tutors at a regional open-admission campus describe their shift to remote synchronous tutoring during COVID-19, from summer 2020 through spring 2021. Technology problems, blurred work-life boundaries, and mental strain made the work hard, and their long collaboration helped them keep going.
notes: Issue 6.1 (Winter 2022). All authors Kent State University. Per author bios: Emily Tondy, graduate student tutor; Alyssa Gelet, undergraduate honors student tutor; Ana Wetzl, English faculty and former Learning Center English Coordinator. Undergraduate co-author. About 7,000 words. License basis: journal-wide CC BY-NC-ND 4.0 statement.

title: Communicating Work-Related Conflict: Textual Analysis of Politeness Strategies and Linguistic Cues in Tutor Session Notes
summary: Analyzes about 1,160 post-session notes from a small liberal arts college writing center for hedging, boosting, and politeness strategies that signal role conflict. Conflict often surfaces in indirect, non-constructive language, and the authors recommend discussing conflict more directly in notes and tutor training.
notes: Issue 7.2 (Spring 2023). Both authors Middlebury College. The article describes the authors as a student and a faculty member and says the research began as a project in a tutor training course; which author was the student is not stated (Giaimo is the writing center director). Useful model of undergraduate-faculty collaborative research. About 7,000-8,000 words. License basis: journal-wide CC BY-NC-ND 4.0 statement.

title: Generative AI Tutor Education in Our Writing Center: A Slow Approach
summary: Describes a Tufts writing center's deliberately slow tutor-education plan for generative AI, built from a 2024 survey of undergraduate Writing Fellows and graduate consultants. The plan uses discussion and hands-on activities, such as a mock session with an AI-generated essay, to build critical AI literacy and clarify tutors' role in academic integrity.
notes: Issue 9.1 (Spring 2025, per the issues archive). Both authors Tufts University; roles not stated on the page. About 3,000-3,500 words. Landing URL is the WordPress short link that resolves on the legacy site; also indexed on the WAC Clearinghouse. License basis: journal-wide CC BY-NC-ND 4.0 statement.

title: Duoethnographic Explorations of Reciprocal Mentorship Between a Writing Center Administrator and a Peer Tutor
summary: A peer tutor and a writing center administrator use duoethnography to examine how co-mentorship supports the growth of tutors, many of them L1.5 writers. They also look at how an Instagram post celebrating that mentorship raised the center's visibility.
notes: Issue 10.2 (Winter 2026). Both authors Florida International University. Galiano was an undergraduate tutor at the time of the study (now a graduate student); Jiang is the administrator. About 8,000-9,000 words. License basis: journal-wide CC BY-NC-ND 4.0 statement on the same site.

title: "It's not what you say; it's how you say it": Writing Center Tutors and Their Conceptualizations of Academic Writing in Tutoring Sessions
summary: Embedded case study of three tutors at one mid-Atlantic writing center and how they talk about academic language. The tutors framed academic writing as professor-driven grammar rules while also valuing student voice, and the author argues for a more linguistically just idea of "sounding academic."
notes: Issue 10.2 (Winter 2026). Author affiliation: Salisbury University; the study comes from the author's dissertation pilot (graduate student author). About 6,000 words. License basis: journal-wide CC BY-NC-ND 4.0 statement.

title: WLN: A Journal of Writing Center Scholarship
summary: Open-access, peer-reviewed journal of writing center scholarship (formerly the Writing Lab Newsletter) known for short practitioner articles and a Tutors' Column in each issue. The full archive from Vol. 1 (1977-1978) is free on the WAC Clearinghouse.

summary: Describes a collaboration that paired tutors-in-training with first-year multilingual writers.

title: The People Make the Place: Reminding Tutors of Their Value in a World of Artificial Intelligence

summary: A Tutors' Column making the case for the value human tutors bring to writers in an age of artificial intelligence.

title: Supporting Hard-of-Hearing and Deaf Writers

summary: A Tutors' Column on how tutors can support hard-of-hearing and Deaf writers in sessions.

title: The CDC Clear Communication Index

Score sheets: https://www.cdc.gov/ccindex/pdf/full-index-score-sheet.pdf and modified-index-score-sheet.pdf. Page last reviewed May 2025. title: Crisis & Emergency Risk Communication (CERC) Manual
authors: Centers for Disease Control and Prevention
publisher_platform: CDC (U.S. Department of Health and Human Services)
summary: CDC's evidence-based manual for organizations communicating during emergencies, with chapters on the psychology of a crisis, messages and audiences, community engagement, communication plans, spokespersons, and working with the media.

title: Messages and Audiences
authors: Centers for Disease Control and Prevention
summary: Explains how to shape crisis messages for different audiences so that people can understand them and act on them.

title: The Psychology of a Crisis
authors: Centers for Disease Control and Prevention
summary: Describes how people take in and act on information under stress during a crisis, and what that means for communicators.
notes: Chapter updated 2019. Public domain per CDC policy.

title: Plain Language Guide Series
summary: The federal government's plain language guidance, in sections on principles, writing for understanding, design for understanding, and testing for understanding.
notes: Adapted from PlainLanguage.gov (plainlanguage.gov/guidelines now redirects here; archive at github.com/gsa/plainlanguage.gov). Digital.gov policies: 'Most material on Digital.gov is free of copyright and may be copied and distributed without permission'; some images are restricted.

title: Communicating Science Effectively: A Research Agenda
authors: National Academies of Sciences, Engineering, and Medicine
summary: A consensus report that reviews what is known about communicating science on contentious public issues and sets out a research agenda covering psychological, cultural, political, and media factors.
notes: DOI 10.17226/23674. Committee chaired by Alan I. Leshner. PDF download offered free as guest download (login or guest checkout). Footer: '(c) National Academy of Sciences. All Rights Reserved.' Link only.

title: The Conversation (U.S. edition)
summary: A nonprofit news site where academic researchers write short articles about their fields for general readers, edited by journalists; a deep source of model texts for writing about research for the public.
notes: Republishing guidelines: articles may be republished under 'Creative Commons — Attribution/No Derivatives license' (CC BY-ND 4.0); credit authors and The Conversation, link back, include the page-view counter, no substantive edits; images are not covered.

title: Scientists may be overestimating the amount of microplastics in the environment – and the culprit is lab gloves
summary: Two researchers explain for general readers how contamination from lab gloves can inflate measurements of microplastics, a public-facing account of how scientists catch errors in their own methods.
notes: Dated March 26, 2026 on topic listing. License per site-wide republishing guidelines; summary based on the headline.

title: An ultrathin coating for electronics looked like a miracle insulator − but a hidden leak fooled researchers for over a decade
summary: A researcher's account, for general readers, of how a measurement artifact made a coating look like a far better insulator than it was, and how the field eventually caught it.
notes: Dated January 19, 2026 on topic listing. License per site-wide republishing guidelines; summary based on the headline. Pairs with readings on peer review and self-correction in science.

title: Soundwriting Pedagogies
authors: Danforth, Courtney S.; Stedman, Kyle D.; Faris, Michael J.
publisher_platform: Computers and Composition Digital Press / Utah State University Press
summary: An edited digital collection of webtexts, each with audio and transcripts, on teaching students to compose with sound: podcasts across a writing program, listening pedagogies, Deaf and hearing perspectives on sound, radio history, and soundwriting as resistance.
notes: Editors. Book page: licensed CC BY-NC 4.0 'with the exception of chapter 6, Sleight of Ear, whose authors retain their copyright.' Year from CCDP catalog listing. Audio-only playlist version also available.

title: Recasting Writing, Voicing Bodies: Podcasts Across a Writing Curriculum
summary: Reflects on bringing a story-driven podcasting project into a large first-year composition program taught mostly by graduate TAs, and on how it unsettled assumptions about what counts as writing and how to assess it.
notes: Chapter 2. Book-level license (chapter 6 excepted). Browser title reads 'Podcasts Across a Writing Program'.

title: Do You Hear What I Hear? A Hearing Teacher and a Deaf Student Negotiate Sound
summary: A co-authored multimodal account by a hearing teacher and a Deaf student in an undergraduate multimodal composition course, arguing that hearing-centered ideas of sound limit who can take part in soundwriting.
notes: Chapter 1; student co-author. Book-level license.

title: Transfer across Media: Using Digital Video in the Teaching of Writing
publisher_platform: Computers and Composition Digital Press / Utah State University Press
summary: A digital book, built around video, that follows students and instructors in composition and basic writing courses to show how composing digital video builds functional, critical, and rhetorical literacies and supports transfer.
notes: ISBN 9781646421077. License basis: footer link to creativecommons.org/licenses/by-nc-nd/4.0/legalcode (no written statement). Year from CCDP catalog. Includes a section on copyright and fair use and appendices with video unit materials.

title: The Archive as Classroom: Pedagogical Approaches to the Digital Archive of Literacy Narratives
authors: Comer, Kathryn; Harker, Michael; McCorkle, Ben
summary: An edited collection on teaching with the Digital Archive of Literacy Narratives (DALN), organized around digital, archive, literacy, and narrative, with appendices of assignment prompts.
notes: Editors. Footer shows both '(cc) BY 4.0' and 'All rights reserved'; recorded as CC BY 4.0, but confirm before adapting. Year from CCDP catalog.

title: Undergraduate Research in Writing Studies: Using the DALN to Stimulate Inquiry and Teach Research Methods
summary: Describes an assignment sequence in which students treat DALN literacy narratives as data for original research, from project design through coding and analysis to a final essay.
notes: Footer shows '(cc) BY 4.0' alongside 'All rights reserved'.

title: Visualizing Captions and Subtitles: The Embodiment of Accessible Multimodal Communication
publisher_platform: Computers and Composition Digital Press / Utah State University Press
summary: A study of captions and subtitles as embodied, designed parts of multimodal communication, written from a Deaf studies and accessibility perspective.
notes: ISBN 978-1-64642-898-4. Page: 'This work is licensed under a Creative Commons Attribution-NonCommercial-NoDerivatives 4.0 International License.' Available as PDF, EPUB, and HTML from the landing page. Year from CCDP catalog listing.

title: Composing with AI
publisher_platform: Computers and Composition Digital Press / Utah State University Press
summary: An edited collection on generative AI in writing studies: histories of disruptive writing technologies, AI policies, classroom reports, text-to-image composing, and teaching AI literacies.

title: Racial Shorthand: Coded Discrimination Contested in Social Media
summary: An edited digital collection analyzing racial coding in social media and popular culture, with chapters on #BlackLivesMatter on Twitter, Barbie's social media, translation as technology, and Latinx digital testimonio.
notes: Editors. Free to read online; no license statement found on landing page. Year from CCDP catalog.

title: The New Work of Composing
authors: Journet, Debra; Ball, Cheryl E.; Trauman, Ryan
publisher_platform: Computers and Composition Digital Press / Utah State University Press
summary: An early born-digital edited collection of twelve chapters on multimodal composing and scholarship, with a foreword by N. Katherine Hayles and responses by Marilyn Cooper, Paul Prior, Diana George, and Andrea Lunsford.
notes: Editors. Free to read online; no license statement found on landing page.

title: Writing Workflows
publisher_platform: University of Michigan Press / Sweetland Digital Rhetoric Collaborative
summary: A web-based book on how writers build and reflect on their technological workflows, the tools and habits that shape a writing process beyond the word processor.
notes: Site: 'This work is licensed under a Creative Commons Attribution-NonCommercial-NoDerivatives 4.0 International License.' Year from the Digital Rhetoric Collaborative series list. The book may carry a subtitle not captured here.

title: Bound by Law? Tales from the Public Domain
authors: Aoki, Keith; Boyle, James; Jenkins, Jennifer
publisher_platform: Duke Center for the Study of the Public Domain
summary: A comic book that follows a documentary filmmaker trying to work out what she can use under copyright and fair use, explaining the public domain and fair use along the way.

First released 2006; a Duke University Press edition followed (year not confirmed this session).

title: Theft! A History of Music
publisher_platform: Duke Center for the Study of the Public Domain
summary: A graphic novel history of musical borrowing and the laws that have tried to control it, from Plato to hip hop sampling.
notes: Footer: Creative Commons Attribution-NonCommercial-ShareAlike 3.0 United States License. Free PDF via https://cspd.law.duke.edu/musiccomic/download/. Keith Aoki credited with initial sketches. Year inferred from 2017 uploads and review on the page.

title: Remix: Making Art and Commerce Thrive in the Hybrid Economy

summary: Lessig's argument that 'read/write' remix culture is a valuable form of expression that copyright law criminalizes, with proposals for reform.

title: Free Culture

notes: Author page: available free under a Creative Commons license; reuse for non-commercial purposes with credit; links by-nc/1.0. Title as listed on the author's page (subtitle omitted). Year not stated on page.

title: The Public Domain: Enclosing the Commons of the Mind

summary: A legal scholar's account of how intellectual property expansion is enclosing the public domain, written for general readers.

summary: A beginner-friendly guide to making charts, maps, and tables with free tools, including chapters on questioning data, detecting misleading visuals and bias, and telling a data story.

title: How to Lie with Charts

notes: Chapter 15. Book-level license.

notes: LibreTexts license tag CC BY-NC 4.0. Last modified July 2025; publication year not shown.

title: Writing the Literature Review
authors: Lloyd, Robert; Mertens, Daniel; Vollrath, Matthew
summary: A brief guide to the literature review that uses upper-level business courses as its main example, with chapters on purpose, process, dissecting a sample review, and academic language.

title: Dissection of a literature review
authors: Lloyd, Robert; Mertens, Daniel; Vollrath, Matthew
summary: Walks through a sample literature review to show how its parts are built.
notes: Chapter 4. Book-level license.

title: Writing and the Sciences: An Anthology
publisher_platform: Alaska Digital Texts (University of Alaska Pressbooks)

title: Journal Articles

notes: Book-level license from Pressbooks metadata.

title: Social Media

notes: Book-level license from Pressbooks metadata.

title: Science Communication Toolkit

title: Inclusive Science Communication
authors: Gupta, Aditi; Harding, Katie; Talluri, Sree Gayathri

notes: Book-level license from Pressbooks metadata.

authors: Peters, Jason; Bates, Jennifer; Martin-Elston, Erin; Johann, Sadie; Maples, Rebekah; Regan, Anne; White, Morgan
summary: A curated collection on argument in STEM fields: stasis theory, rhetorical appeals, Toulmin, information literacy, research writing, data visualization, writing for STEM and health-sciences audiences, and genres such as analytical reports, proposals, and health-sciences literature reviews.
notes: License page: 'licensed under a Creative Commons Attribution-ShareAlike 4.0 International License, except where otherwise noted.' Curated from other OER (front matter calls the authors curators), so individual chapters may carry their source licenses. Useful for a STEM-themed FYC or argument course.

authors: Peters, Jason; Bates, Jennifer; Martin-Elston, Erin; Johann, Sadie; Maples, Rebekah; Regan, Anne; White, Morgan

authors: Peters, Jason; Bates, Jennifer; Martin-Elston, Erin; Johann, Sadie; Maples, Rebekah; Regan, Anne; White, Morgan
summary: Summarizes principles for choosing and designing charts and graphs that support an argument honestly.

authors: Chatterjee, Karishma; Ricks, Damla; Waryas Hughey, Diane E.

title: Preparing to Publish
authors: Huffman, Sarah; Cotos, Elena; Becker, Kimberly

authors: Huffman, Sarah; Cotos, Elena; Becker, Kimberly
